general: Seedling disease appearing within a month of sowing
Patches of dead seedlings at the primary leaf stage
Seedlings turn slightly chlorotic before dying
Rotting in the collar region covered with white mycelial growth
Seedlings uprooted easily with lower root remaining in soil
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of dead seedlings scattered over the field

field_identification: White or brown sclerotial bodies attached to the collar region or in the soil around dead seedlings
Rotting in collar region covered with white mycelial growth
differential_diagnosis: Differentiated from seedling diseases caused by Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or Pythium by white mycelial growth on the rotting collar region

causes_and_risk_factors: Undecomposed organic matter left on seedbeds
Pigeonpea following cereal crops like sorghum without clearing stubble

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: High soil moisture at sowing
other_conditions: Early-sown (June) crops more affected than later-sown crops in India

severity_and_yield_loss: A minor disease that can cause severe losses when undecomposed organic matter is left on the surface of seedbeds

cultural_management: Deep summer ploughing
Select well drained fields
Keep the fields free from un-decomposed organic matter
Sow when soil moisture is low
Select fields where cereal crops (such as sorghum) have not been grown during the previous season
Collect cereal stubble from the field and destroy it before sowing pigeonpea

documents.causal_agent: Phytophthora drechsleri Tucker f. sp. cajani

general: Resembles damping off disease causing seedlings to die suddenly
Water-soaked lesions on leaves
Brown to black, slightly sunken lesions on stems and petioles
Infected leaves lose turgidity and become desiccated
Lesions girdle main stems or branches causing them to break and foliage above to dry up
Production of large galls on stems especially at edges of lesions in plants not killed
Infects foliage and stems but not the root system
visual_field_symptoms: Leaves large gaps in plant stands
Appears first in low-lying areas of fields where water temporarily stagnates

field_identification: Water-soaked leaf lesions
Brown to black slightly sunken stem/petiole lesions
Stem breakage at infection point with stem galls

causes_and_risk_factors: Soilborne fungus surviving as chlamydospores, oospores, and dormant mycelium
Thick canopy of short-duration types and close spacing (30 x 10 cm)
Higher genetic susceptibility
Wild relative Cajanus scarabaeoides var. scarabaeoides is a host

favorable_conditions.humidity: Warm and humid weather following infection results in rapid development
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: More common on Alfisols than Vertisols; low-lying areas where water temporarily stagnates
other_conditions: Continuous leaf wetness for eight hours required for infection

disease_development_and_spread: Wind and rain help disseminate zoospores and facilitate infection through plant damage
epidemiology: Plants gradually develop tolerance as they grow older and are not infected after 60 days of age
severity_and_yield_loss: A devastating disease that kills young (1-7-week-old) plants
Yield losses usually higher in short duration pigeonpea than medium- and long-duration types

cultural_management: Early or normal sowing
Practice ridge planting methods
Summer solarization and summer ploughing should be done
Select fields with no previous record of blight
Avoid sowing pigeonpea in fields with low-lying patches that are prone to waterlogging
Prepare raised seed beds and provide good drainage
Use wide inter-row spacing

chemical_management.timing: Two sprays at 15-day intervals starting from 15 days after germination

general: Patches of dead plants in the field when flowering or podding
Purple band extending upwards from the base of the main stem (more easily seen in green stems)
Partial wilting of the plant (associated with lateral root infection), distinct from total wilt (tap root infection)
Browning of stem tissue in the region of the purple band
Browning or blackening of xylem when stem/primary branches are split open
Die-back symptoms on lower branches with purple band extending from tip downwards and internal xylem blackening
Leaf symptoms before death: loss of leaf turgidity, inter-veinal clearing, chlorosis to bright yellow leaves
early_symptoms: Sometimes occur earlier when plants are 1-2 months old (may lack purple band but show internal browning/blackening)
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of dead plants in the field during flowering or podding

field_identification: Purple band on main stem
Partial or total wilting
Browning/blackening of xylem upon splitting stems
differential_diagnosis: Distinguished from termite damage, drought, and Phytophthora blight (which kill the whole plant) by partial wilting

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed and soilborne fungus surviving on infected plant debris in soil for up to 10 years
Long- and medium-duration types suffer more than short-duration types
Ratooning predisposes plants to wilt

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: More severe on Vertisols than on Alfisols
other_conditions: Early sowing, good weed management, and good crop growth encourage wilt development
Pigeonpeas intercropped with sorghum are less attacked by wilt than sole-cropped plants

severity_and_yield_loss: Annual losses estimated at US$71 million in India and US$5 million in eastern Africa

cultural_management: Collect and burn plant residues after harvesting
Do summer ploughing
Select a field with no previous record of wilt for at least 3 years
Select seed from disease-free fields
Grow pigeonpea intercropped or mixed with cereal crops, eg, sorghum
Rotate pigeonpea with sorghum, tobacco, or castor every 3 years
Uproot wilted plants and use them for fuelwood
Solarize the field in summer to help reduce inoculum

documents.causal_agent: Rhizoctonia bataticola (Taub.) Butler, Macrophomina phaseolina (Tassi) Goidanich

general: Infected plants suddenly and prematurely dry up
Rotten and shredded roots
Finer roots affected with dark, blackened streaks underneath bark with dark sclerotial bodies
Brittle roots that break when touched
Root rotting extends to base of stem under hot, humid conditions
Spindle-shaped lesions on stems and branches with light gray centers, brown margins, and scattered pycnidial bodies
Lesions coalesce causing branches or whole plants to dry up and die
visual_field_symptoms: Suddenly and prematurely dried up plants

field_identification: Rotten and shredded roots with dark sclerotial bodies
Spindle-shaped stem lesions with light gray centers

causes_and_risk_factors: Serious problem in late-sown or summer crops and in perennial or ratooned pigeonpeas
Affects short-duration pigeonpeas sown in rainy season
Crops more susceptible in reproductive stage than vegetative stage

favorable_conditions.humidity: Hot and dry weather encourage development; hot, humid conditions extend root rotting to stem base
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Rain after a prolonged dry spell predisposes plants to disease
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: More prevalent on Vertisols than on Alfisols

cultural_management: Disease incidence can be reduced if previous crop stubble is buried deep and allowed to decompose well before pigeonpea is sown
Select fields with no previous record of dry root rot
Avoid sowing late so that crop escapes drought and high temperatures at maturity

general: Normally seen at advanced stages of plant growth
Initial stem lesions with gray centers and dark brown margins containing pycnidia
Lesions coalesce and girdle the stem, developing into large swollen cankers leading to premature plant death
early_symptoms: Lesions on stems with gray centers and dark brown margins containing pycnidia
advanced_symptoms: Large swollen cankers girdling the stem leading to premature plant death
visual_field_symptoms: Large cankers on stem

field_identification: Large swollen cankers on stems with pycnidia

cultural_management: Avoid fields with previous records of the disease
Remove infected plants to reduce the build-up of inoculum in the soil

Waterlogged roots are rotten, foul-smelling, bark easy to peel off
Brown patches with wavy margins in collar region (seen when bark is peeled off)
Reddish brown discontinuous streaks in the wood
visual_field_symptoms: Dead plants in field without external stem symptoms

field_identification: Brown patches with wavy margins in collar region
Reddish brown discontinuous streaks in wood
Rotten, foul-smelling roots with easily peeling bark
differential_diagnosis: Can be confused with wilt or Phytophthora blight, but distinguished by brown patches with wavy margins in collar region and reddish brown discontinuous streaks in wood

causes_and_risk_factors: Highly susceptible to waterlogging

severity_and_yield_loss: Can result in sudden death of plants

documents.disease_name: Bacterial Leaf Spot and Stem Canker
documents.causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. cajani (Kulkarni, Patel & Abhyankar) Dye

general: Small necrotic spots surrounded by bright yellow halos on lower leaves (about 1 month old)
Rough, raised, cankerous lesions appear on the stem
Leaf spots do not usually cause defoliation
Cankers can cause stems to break, but broken part usually remains attached
Stem cankers increase in size up to 15-25 cm long
Severe infection causes affected branches to dry
early_symptoms: Small necrotic spots surrounded by bright yellow halos on lower leaves of ~1 month old plants
advanced_symptoms: Stem cankers increasing in size up to 15-25 cm long
Drying of affected branches in severe infections
visual_field_symptoms: Broken stems with cankerous lesions
Enlarged stem cankers

field_identification: Necrotic leaf spots with bright yellow halos
Raised cankerous stem lesions and broken stems

causes_and_risk_factors: African germplasm more susceptible than Indian germplasm
Pigeonpea with purple stems less susceptible to stem canker than those with green stems
Leaf infection at all stages, stem infection usually in younger plants

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Appears in India in rainy season (July and August)
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Incidence generally higher in low-lying waterlogged areas than well-drained areas

cultural_management: Select well-drained fields
Select seed from healthy crops

documents.causal_agent: Oidiopsis taurica (Lev.) Salmon (Teleomorph: Leveillula taurica [Lev.] Arnaud)

general: White powdery fungal growths on aerial parts (leaves, flowers, pods)
Stunting of young plants followed by white powdery growth before flowering stage
Initial small chlorotic spots on upper leaf surface, followed by white powdery patches on corresponding lower surfaces
Powdery growth covers entire lower leaf surface upon sporulation
Severe infections result in heavy defoliation
early_symptoms: Small chlorotic spots on upper surface of individual leaves
advanced_symptoms: White powdery patches on lower surfaces covering the entire lower leaf surface
Heavy defoliation in severe infections
visual_field_symptoms: Defoliation in severely affected plants

field_identification: White powdery fungal growth on leaves, flowers, and pods
Chlorotic spots on upper leaf surface with powdery patches underneath

causes_and_risk_factors: Polycyclic disease (initial infection and secondary spread)
Infection directly proportional to conidia inoculum quantity
Indian varieties with thin, succulent leaves more susceptible than Kenyan varieties with thick leaves
Plants attacked by sterility mosaic or phyllody support abundant sporulation and act as continuous source of inoculum
Survives on perennial pigeonpeas, volunteer plants in shade, ratoon growth of stubbles, and as dormant mycelium on axillary buds
Early sowing and irrigation in India encourage establishment

favorable_conditions.humidity: Cool, humid climate congenial for infection/colonization; warm humid climate good for sporulation/spore dispersal

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas affected with the disease that are a source of inoculum
Sow late (after July) in India, to reduce disease incidence

documents.causal_agent: Cercospora cajani Hennings (most prevalent), Cercospora indica Singh, Cercospora instabilis Rangel, Cercospora thirumalacharii Sharma & Mishra (Teleomorph: Mycovellosiella cajani [Henn.] Rangel ex Trotter)

general: Small circular to irregular necrotic spots or lesions usually on older leaves
Lesions coalesce causing leaf blight and defoliation
During epidemics, lesions appear on young branches causing tips to dry and die
Indian isolates produce fluffy mycelial growth on lesions, African isolates produce concentric zonations
early_symptoms: Small circular to irregular necrotic spots on older leaves
advanced_symptoms: Lesions coalesce causing leaf blight and defoliation
Drying of branch tips during epidemics
visual_field_symptoms: Small necrotic spots on older leaves
Concentric zonation on leaf

field_identification: Small necrotic spots on older leaves
Concentric zonations (African isolates) or fluffy mycelial growth (Indian isolates)

causes_and_risk_factors: More common in long-duration and perennial pigeonpeas grown in eastern Africa

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Cyclonic rains in southern and north-eastern peninsular India result in sudden outbreaks in certain years
other_conditions: Normally appears when plants are flowering and podding

severity_and_yield_loss: A problem in humid regions
Yield losses up to 85% reported from eastern Africa
Losses are severe when defoliation occurs before flowering and podding

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas that are a source of inoculum
Select seed from healthy crops

documents.causal_agent: Alternaria sp, Alternaria tenuissima (Kunze ex Persoon) Wiltshire, Alternaria alternata (Fries) Keissler

general: Small, circular, necrotic spots on leaves that develop quickly forming typically concentric rings
Lesions appear on all aerial plant parts including flowers, flower buds, and pods
Blighting of leaves, severe defoliation, and drying of infected branches
early_symptoms: Small, circular, necrotic spots on leaves
advanced_symptoms: Concentric rings on spots, blighting of leaves, severe defoliation, and drying of infected branches
visual_field_symptoms: Necrotic spot on leaf
Drying of flowers and flower buds

field_identification: Circular necrotic spots with concentric rings on leaves and floral parts

causes_and_risk_factors: Emerging disease under climate change scenario
Not serious in rainy-season crops sown at normal time, but causes problems in crops sown late (September) or in postrainy season on plains of north-eastern India
Seed infection only reported from Puerto Rico

favorable_conditions.humidity: Warm, humid conditions favor fungal sporulation

cultural_management: Avoid fields close to perennial pigeonpeas
Select seed from healthy crops
Sow early

general: Round, necrotic spots up to 10 mm in diameter on leaves
Lesions have wavy dark brown margins with gray centers, containing characteristically concentric rings of pycnidial bodies
Severe infections result in desiccation and defoliation
early_symptoms: Round, necrotic spots up to 10 mm in diameter
advanced_symptoms: Concentric rings of pycnidial bodies, desiccation, and defoliation in severe infections
visual_field_symptoms: Necrotic leaf spots with pycnidial bodies

field_identification: Round necrotic leaf spots with wavy dark brown margins, gray centers, and concentric rings of pycnidia

favorable_conditions.humidity: Mean humidity range of 73-80% favors severe outbreaks
other_conditions: Problem in warm, humid climates; appears usually in July and persists throughout cropping season; serious epidemics in October in north-eastern plains of India

general: Problem on pigeonpea crops in north-eastern hills of India
Dark brown, circular to elliptical lesions (2-10 mm diameter) originating on leaf margins
Lesions coalesce to form dark brown patches
Infected leaves become yellow and dry prematurely
White mycelia with abundant conidia appear on blighted leaves under humid weather

advanced_symptoms: Coalescence into dark brown patches, premature yellowing and drying

general: Starts with marginal chlorosis and progresses to 'burning' of leaf laminae margins
Commonly observed late in the season
Starts in lower leaves and progresses upwards
early_symptoms: Marginal chlorosis on lower leaves
advanced_symptoms: Burning of leaf laminae margins progressing upwards
visual_field_symptoms: Margins of leaf laminae showing burnt appearance

field_identification: Marginal chlorosis and burning of leaf margins on lower leaves progressing upwards
differential_diagnosis: Distinguished from fungal leaf blights by systematic nature and absence of chlorotic area between dried and healthy portions of laminae

general: Patches of bushy, pale green plants without flowers or pods in the field
Leaves are small and show light and dark green mosaic pattern
Initial mosaic symptoms appear as vein-clearing on young leaves
Infection at 45 days after emergence or later may show symptoms on only some parts while rest appear normal
Some varieties (e.g., ICP 2376) exhibit ring spot leaf symptoms (green islands in chlorotic areas) producing normal flowers and pods
Strains in Bihar (India) and Nepal cause severe internodal shortening, clustering of branches, and filiform leaves
early_symptoms: Vein-clearing on young leaves
advanced_symptoms: Bushy pale green plants without flowers or pods, small leaves with light/dark green mosaic pattern
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of bushy pale green plants in the field
Infected plants without flowers and pods
Vein clearing symptom on young leaves
Infected leaf with ring spot symptom

field_identification: Patches of bushy, pale green plants lacking flowers/pods
Mosaic pattern, vein-clearing, or ring spot symptoms on small leaves

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: Eriophyid mite Aceria cajani Channabasavanna
Pathogen and mite vector are specific to Cajanus cajan and wild relative C. scarabaeoides var. scarabaeoides
Perennial/volunteer pigeonpeas and ratooned growth provide reservoirs for mite and pathogen

favorable_conditions.temperature: Symptoms suppressed during hot summer months, reappear with monsoon rains
favorable_conditions.humidity: Shade and humidity encourage mite multiplication, especially in hot summer weather
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Monsoon rains bring back symptom expression
other_conditions: High disease incidence when pigeonpeas are inter- or mixed cropped with sorghum or millets

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by eriophyid mite Aceria cajani
Mites can be wind-borne up to 2 km from inoculum source
severity_and_yield_loss: A serious problem in Nepal and India, estimated to cause annual pigeonpea grain losses worth US$282 million

cultural_management: Spacing between lines should be maintained at 30 to 40 cms
Weeds should be rouged out at their inception
Maintain timely sowing of the crop
Select a field well away from perennial or ratoon pigeonpeas
Destroy sources of sterility mosaic inoculum, i.e., perennial or ratooned pigeonpeas
Uproot infected plants at an early stage of disease development and destroy them
Rotate crops to reduce sources of inoculum and mite vectors

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: acaricide or insecticides like Kelthane®, Morestan®, metasystox
chemical_management.timing: Early stages of plant growth to control mite vector

general: Green and golden yellow mosaic mottle symptoms on leaves
Sometimes affected parts of leaves become necrotic
Diseased plants usually scattered in field, produce fewer pods than normal when infected early
visual_field_symptoms: Green and golden yellow mosaic mottle symptoms on leaves

field_identification: Green and golden yellow mosaic mottle symptoms on leaves

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: White fly Bemisia tabaci Gennadius
Off-season and isolated sowings suffer more because pigeonpea is not a preferred host of whitefly vectors (feed only when forced by absence of other host plants)

cultural_management: Avoid sowing late to reduce disease severity
Uproot and burn infected plants if disease appears on isolated plants in field

general: Excessive proliferation and clustering of branches with small pale green leaves giving a 'witches' broom' appearance
Plants rarely produce flowers and pods
Flowers, if produced, appear in clusters with elongated pedicels
Whole or part of plant may exhibit symptoms depending on intensity
visual_field_symptoms: Clustering of branches with small pale green leaves

field_identification: Excessive branch proliferation and clustering with small pale green leaves ('witches' broom')

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: Leaf hopper Empoasca sp

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas affected with witches' broom
Pull out and destroy any infected plants to minimize secondary spread of disease
Avoid ratoon cropping

Flowers are converted into leafy structures
visual_field_symptoms: Floral proliferation (bushy plants with axillary proliferation of phylloid flowers)

field_identification: Bushy plants with flowers converted into leafy structures (phylloid flowers) at flowering

general: Aerial parts show no characteristic symptoms, but reduced plant vigor, delayed flowering (in whole or patches), and leaf yellowing indicate infestation
Root galls (knots) are most characteristic symptom visible with naked eye
Examining roots for egg sacs useful when galls are very small
visual_field_symptoms: Infected plants show stunted growth in the field
Root galls

field_identification: Root galls (knots) on main and lateral roots
Stunted growth and leaf yellowing
diagnostic_methods: Examining roots for the presence of egg sacs when galls are very small

causes_and_risk_factors: Meloidogyne incognita and M. javanica widely distributed in tropical/subtropical climates
Wide host range in extensive soil types; crop damage reflective of sandy soils or sandy patches
Weed hosts help maintain high nematode populations
Combined infestations of M. javanica and M. incognita increase severity
Infection increases severity of Fusarium wilt infection

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy soils or sandy patches within fields

severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses of 8 to 35% reported from Caribbean, Africa, and southeast Asia

cultural_management: Select field with no previous record of nematode infestation
Rotate pigeonpea with wheat to reduce nematode populations
Solarize soil in summer to reduce nematode populations

general: Poor and stunted plants evident 30-45 days after sowing
Minute, pearl-like, white females of H. cajani attached to roots visible with naked eye or hand lens (10x)
Nematode infestation can delay flowering and pod formation for more than a week
visual_field_symptoms: Infected plants show stunted growth in the field
Infected roots with pearl-like female nematodes

field_identification: Minute pearl-like white females attached to roots
diagnostic_methods: Observation of females through hand lens (10x)

causes_and_risk_factors: Host range largely confined to Leguminosae, with Sesamum indicum and Phyllanthus maderaspatensis as non-legume hosts
Widespread in sandy loam soils in northern India and black cotton soils in western and southern India
Lives up to 45 cm deep in soil throughout the year
Infestation enhances aggressiveness of Fusarium udum infection in wilt-susceptible pigeonpeas

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy loam soils in northern India and black cotton soils in western and southern India

epidemiology: Summer fallowing reduces densities of H. cajani by 45% at 0-15 cm but does not affect densities at lower soil depths

cultural_management: Select fields with no previous record of nematode infestation
Rotate crops with sorghum, maize, or pearl millet to reduce nematode populations
Solarize soil in summer to reduce nematode populations

general: Infected plants grow less vigorously than healthy ones with smaller root systems
Egg masses covered with soil found on roots upon uprooting
Roots appear dirty because soil particles adhere to mucilaginous nematode egg sacs and are not easily dislodged by shaking
visual_field_symptoms: Plants stunted due to dirty root disease
Infected roots with egg masses

field_identification: Roots appearing dirty due to soil particles adhering to mucilaginous egg masses not dislodged by shaking
diagnostic_methods: Dipping roots in 0.25% trypan blue and rinsing in water selectively colors nematode egg sacs blue while roots are not stained (identifies reniform nematode without microscope)

causes_and_risk_factors: Attacks many crops in 38 subtropical and tropical countries; extensive host range
Can reduce number of Rhizobium nodules produced
Wilt-susceptible genotypes die prematurely when nematode and wilt fungus are both present

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy and red soils (Alfisols) in western and southern India; variable crop growth in northern India
other_conditions: Damage thresholds range from pre-plant nematode densities of 1.0 to 4.0 cm-3 of soil

disease_development_and_spread: Can survive in absence of host for more than 300 days without losing infectivity
epidemiology: Summer fallowing reduces R. reniformis densities to 70% at 0-15 cm soil depth and 36% at 15-30 cm soil depth
severity_and_yield_loss: Infestation severely affects pigeonpea production in Fiji

cultural_management: Select fields with no previous record of nematode infestation
Rotate crops with rice, maize, or groundnut to reduce nematode populations
Solarize soil in summer to reduce nematode populations

general: Ovaries in the inflorescence get converted into black powdery mass (sori) in diseased flowers.
Sori found in common grain position protruding outside between the glumes.
Seed gets replaced with fine grained black spores.
Sori are covered by a thin slimy layer which get ruptured to deliver spores at maturity.
early_symptoms: In the initial stages sori appears to be shiny green in colour that slowly converted into brown to black at ripening.
advanced_symptoms: Sori generally bigger in size (3-4 mm lengthy and 2-3 mm wide) than the seed (1-2mm).
visual_field_symptoms: Black powdery mass replacing grains in panicles.

field_identification: Ovaries converted into black powdery mass (sori) protruding between the glumes.

causes_and_risk_factors: Use of severely infected grains for sowing
Presence of teleutospores in soil

favorable_conditions.temperature: 30 °C is favourable for germination of teleutospore

disease_development_and_spread: Pathogen survives as teleutospore along with infected seeds or in soil.
Primary infection takes place when severely infected grains are used for sowing and air-borne sporidia cause infection.
Infection of floral part takes place during flowering.
It takes 14 days to produce spore after inoculation and sori get ripened within 21 to 28 days.
severity_and_yield_loss: Responsible for 5-30% yield loss in the field.
Severe outbreak causing heavy losses in grain yield/production noticed when commercial F1 hybrids were used.

cultural_management: Deep summer ploughing to incorporate spores deep into the soil.
Inter-cropping with mung bean.
Removal of crop residues and deep summer ploughing or crop rotation with non-host plants to reduce soil-borne inoculum.
biological_management: Use Trichoderma virens (6g/kg seeds) and raw cow milk or raw goat milk (about 18h 50% dilution with water) as seed treatment and treat soil with T. virens (10g/m2).

prevention: Practice clean cultivation like collecting smutted heads in cloth bags and dipping in boiling water.
farmer_action_points: Collect smutted heads in cloth bags and dip in boiling water to kill the pathogen and reduce inoculum.
research_findings: Thiram resulted in good inhibition of the fungus in vitro.
Vitavax and Plantvax effectively suppressed smut.

documents.causal_agent: Puccinia penniseti Zimm. (P. substriata var. indica)

general: Round to elliptical reddish-orange pustule on the leaf.
Distal half of the leaf is infected first and then pustules spread over both the surfaces.
Mature pustules rupture and release rusty spores.
Severely rusted plants look reddish-brown.
early_symptoms: Initial symptoms appear as uredinia pustules with circular and reddish-brown to reddish orange coloured uredospores.
advanced_symptoms: At the later stages, telia replaces uredinia which is black, ovoid, and subepidermal.
Leaves get wilted from top to bottom.
More rust pustules can appear on stems and plants will fall down if disease incidence is higher.
visual_field_symptoms: Reddish-brown to reddish-orange pustules on leaves, severe plants looking reddish-brown.

field_identification: Round to elliptical reddish-orange pustules on leaves releasing rusty spores.

causes_and_risk_factors: Alternate host (brinjal, grasses)
Air-borne spores

favorable_conditions.temperature: Low temperature of 10 to 12 °C required for teliospore germination
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Spell of rainy weather is very favourable for occurrence of disease

disease_development_and_spread: Pathogen survives on alternate host (brinjal, grasses).
Secondary spread takes place by air-borne spores.
severity_and_yield_loss: Appears in later stage of crop growth, usually at seed developing stage after grain-filling, thus causing little loss in grain yield.

biological_management: Biocontrol agents, Aspergillus globosum, Chaetomium globosum and Trichoderma koningii can be used for biological control via seed bio priming, soil application, or foliar spray.

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Found most effective among tested fungicides

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: ICML 11 (land race from Chad, identified as rust resistant)
prevention: Timely removal of alternate hosts (brinjal, grasses).
research_findings: Triadimefon, Hexaconazole and Propiconazole tested for management; Hexaconazole @ 0.1% found most effective.
Trichoderma spp. found very effective in controlling the disease.

alternative_names: Bipolaris leaf spot of pearl millet

general: Small, brown flecks or oval to oblong or rectangular spots on leaves.
Lesions may expand and coalesce.
Lesions usually are tan or greyish brown with a more or less distinct dark brown border.
early_symptoms: Early infection may cause seedling blight.
visual_field_symptoms: Tan or greyish brown lesions with dark brown borders on leaves.

field_identification: Oval, oblong or rectangular spots with tan or greyish brown centres and dark brown borders on leaves.

causes_and_risk_factors: Pathogen survives on crop residues, stray crops, collateral hosts and seed-borne.
disease_development_and_spread: Pathogen survives on crop residues, stray crops, collateral hosts and a few may be seed-borne.
Secondary spread takes place with the help of air-borne conidia.
severity_and_yield_loss: Generally appears in the later stage of the crop when grain filling is almost over, thus of lesser economic importance, though severe loss may occur at early stage.

general: Oval lesion with dark brown margins and pale tan to grey or white centres, dotted with rows of black conidiophores.

documents.causal_agent: Cotton-infecting begomoviruses (family Geminiviridae) with alpha and beta satellites

general: Thickening and darkening of veins seen against sunlight (SVT type)
Upward or downward curling of leaves
Secondary leaf-like structures originating from nectaries (enations)
Stunted growth and dwarf appearance with reduced internodal length
early_symptoms: Small and large vein thickening and darkening on the underside of new leaves
advanced_symptoms: Severe leaf curling, enations on leaves and bracts, extreme stunting
visual_field_symptoms: Stunted plants showing bushy and dwarf appearance with curled leaves on top of the plant and branches

field_identification: Observe new leaves on top of plant for vein thickening and upward/downward curling
diagnostic_methods: Laboratory diagnosis and vector association

causes_and_risk_factors: Spread by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Presence of weed, ornamental, and vegetable alternate hosts (~26 genera)

other_conditions: Presence of vector Bemisia tabaci and alternate hosts

disease_development_and_spread: Spread by whitefly Bemisia tabaci vector; symptoms can appear at seedling stage (~30 DAS) onwards
epidemiology: PDI increases slowly during June and reaches up to 80% during August and September in the north zone.
severity_and_yield_loss: Average yield loss corresponding to disease rating scales 1 to 6 recorded to be 15, 28, 38.6, 49.1, 59.1, and 72.1% in Bt cotton hybrids.

cultural_management: Weed sanitation
Cultivation of Desi cotton/sorghum/pearl millet/maize as border rows
Optimal use of nitrogenous fertilizers
Avoid growing whitefly and CLCuD host crops near cotton

chemical_management.timing: At fortnightly interval starting from 30 days after sowing (3-5 sprays)

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: Butter milk / Cow urine + Calcium nitrate + mustard oil
chemical_management.dose: 5% / cow urine + Calcium nitrate (6.6%+0.5%) or mustard oil (3.0%)

integrated_management: Grow recommended Bt hybrids/varieties resistant/tolerant to CLCuD
Vector management using appropriate insecticides for adults and nymphs

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Recommended Bt hybrids/varieties resistant/tolerant to CLCuD
prevention: Destroy volunteer/ratoon/infected cotton plants and weed hosts
farmer_action_points: Monitor whitefly populations and remove alternate hosts
research_findings: Incidence is increasing in Bt and non-Bt hybrids in the north zone.

documents.causal_agent: Tobacco streak virus (genus Ilarvirus, family Bromoviridae)

general: Chlorosis of young leaves at tip, discoloration, bronzing, necrosis
Veinal chlorosis, curling of leaves, necrotic streaks on petioles, stem, and flowers
Dwarfing or stunting of plants, square drying and dropping
early_symptoms: Acute or necrotic stage: local lesions appear as rings, solid necrotic spots, or diamond-shaped patterns
advanced_symptoms: Chronic stage: leaves thicker than normal with smoother texture, tubular corolla splits with separated bracts
visual_field_symptoms: Necrotic symptoms starting from top to bottom, square drying on plants

field_identification: Observe newer leaves and tips for chlorosis, necrosis, and square drying
differential_diagnosis: Resembles physiological or nutritional disorders and herbicide phytotoxicity

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted through pollen assisted by thrips (Thripidae)
Abundance of infected pollen of parthenium, thrips population and movement

favorable_conditions.temperature: Above 30°C causes severe symptoms like large necrotic arcs, broken rings, lines, and dots
other_conditions: Presence of parthenium weed hosts and thrips vectors

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted via thrips-assisted pollen transfer; asymptomatic infection in weed hosts like parthenium
severity_and_yield_loss: Infection at early or mid-growth stage results in severe reduction in yield and premature plant death. 12.6 to 38.8% occurrence in Tamil Nadu (2010).
farmer_action_points: Manage thrips and remove parthenium weeds
research_findings: Emerging disease in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Maharashtra.

general: Stunting, leaf rolling, intense green foliage, vein yellowing, brittleness of leaves
Reduced flower and boll size, sometimes resulting in plant sterility
visual_field_symptoms: Stunted plants with intense green, rolled leaves starting from top to bottom

field_identification: Check for intense green foliage, leaf rolling, and stunting on newer leaves

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by aphid (Aphis gossypii) in a circulative-persistent manner
disease_development_and_spread: Spread by Aphis gossypii
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses of up to 80% from susceptible cultivars reported in South America.
farmer_action_points: Monitor and control aphid populations
warnings_and_limitations: Biosecurity threat

general: Leaf crumpling, downward curling
Interveinal hypertrophy, foliar mosaic, puckering
Shortening of internodes, stunting
visual_field_symptoms: Stunted plants with crumpled, puckered, and downward-curled leaves

field_identification: Observe leaves for crumpling, puckering, and downward curling without vein thickening
differential_diagnosis: Similar to CLCuD except for small vein darkening and vein thickening

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci
Ratooning (pruning and allowing cotton to regrow)
disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by whitefly
severity_and_yield_loss: Severe outbreaks may be exacerbated by ratooning.

cultural_management: Avoid ratooning

farmer_action_points: Control whitefly, avoid ratooning
warnings_and_limitations: Biosecurity threat
research_findings: Occurs in southwestern USA and Mexico; one early report in Maharashtra, India without further confirmation.

general: Cessation of internode elongation, reduction in leaf size, stunting
Conversion of entire inflorescence into phyllody or malformation
Twisted, rolled leaves with abnormal color, closely arranged on top of stem
Witches' broom symptoms, hairy roots
advanced_symptoms: Dwarfing, resetting, or elongation with early senescence
visual_field_symptoms: Plants showing yellowing, reddening, stunting, and floral malformation

field_identification: Look for floral malformation into leaves, little leaf symptoms, and witches' broom
diagnostic_methods: Sequence comparisons

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by brown leafhopper/jassids Orosius cellulosus
Presence of Sida spp. and Mitracarpus scaber reservoirs

other_conditions: Presence of leafhopper vectors and Sida weed reservoirs

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by leafhopper vectors
epidemiology: In Mali, up to 50% of plants infected in some fields.

cultural_management: Remove Sida weed reservoirs

farmer_action_points: Monitor host plants and insect vectors
warnings_and_limitations: Strict quarantine importance
research_findings: Recorded in Western Africa; little leaf symptoms observed in New Delhi (2010) with homology to 16SrI group.

documents.causal_agent: Rhizoctonia bataticola = Macrophomina phaseolina, Rhizoctonia solani, Sclerotium delphinii, Sclerotium rolfsii

general: Wilting of plant foliage from top to bottom
Leaves remain attached to branches/stem
Dry or wet dark rot of lower stem followed by shredding of bark
Discolored stele and pith, black dot-like sclerotia beneath bark
early_symptoms: Yellow patch on lower stem which later turns black, drying of seedlings
advanced_symptoms: Dissolution of stem and root tissues, minute sclerotia
visual_field_symptoms: Plants wilting in circular patches in the field that expand year after year

field_identification: Check for circular patches of wilted plants, bark shredding at base, and easy pulling from ground

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne fungi surviving in soil and crop debris

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Prevalent in sandy soils, alluvial soils, and heavy clays (black cotton soils)

disease_development_and_spread: Occurs in circular patches; M. phaseolina at seedling stage (60 DAS) or after wood formation; R. solani at 30 DAS and severe at 90-120 DAS
severity_and_yield_loss: Serious in northern India, affects both G. hirsutum and G. arboreum, being more serious in desi cotton.

cultural_management: Crop rotation
Deep ploughing
Incorporation of crop residue
Green manuring
Well-decomposed FYM/compost
biological_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum @ 4 g/kg or T. viride @ 4 g/kg or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg
Soil application of Trichoderma spp. and/or P. fluorescens @ 2.5 kg/ha in 250 kg vermicompost/FYM
integrated_management: Seed treatment combined with soil application of bioagents and spot drenching of Carbendazim

prevention: Avoid planting seeds from infested regions
farmer_action_points: Spot-treat affected patches with Carbendazim or bioagents

general: Wilting of plant foliage from top to bottom
Darkening of veins on cotyledons, peripheral chlorosis and necrosis
Yellowing at margin of lower leaves, chlorosis in patches between main veins
early_symptoms: Darkening of veins on cotyledons at seedling stage
advanced_symptoms: Shedding of all leaves before stem dries out
visual_field_symptoms: Wilting and drying of plants in patches in the field

field_identification: Check for wilting in patches and make a cross-section of stem near root zone to observe xylem color change
diagnostic_methods: Stem cross-section for vascular discoloration

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed and soil-borne fungal pathogen surviving on seed and crop residues via chlamydospores
disease_development_and_spread: Appears generally between 30 to 120 DAS; colonizes roots and grows systemically into vascular tissues
severity_and_yield_loss: Loss may vary from field to field and variety to variety from 5 to 40%.

cultural_management: Crop rotation
integrated_management: Grow resistant diploid varieties (upland cotton/Bt hybrids are immune to Indian race 4 of this pathogen)

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Upland cotton / Bt hybrids are immune to the Indian race of the pathogen
farmer_action_points: Grow resistant upland Bt hybrids where diploid wilt is a problem
warnings_and_limitations: Occurs only in diploid cotton in India
research_findings: Fusarium wilt has become less important as upland cotton is grown in >90% area and is immune to the Indian race.

general: Drooping branches and leaves
Interveinal chlorosis followed by yellowing, leaf scorching
Drying of leaf margins and areas between veins ("Tiger stripe symptoms")
Defoliation, plant death, flecked brown or pink discoloration of vascular tissues
advanced_symptoms: Death of entire plant, smaller bolls, pinkish discoloration in stem and wood
visual_field_symptoms: Wilted plants showing tiger stripe leaf symptoms and vascular discoloration

field_identification: Check for tiger stripe leaf symptoms and cut stem cross/diagonally at base to observe brown/pink vascular discoloration
diagnostic_methods: Cutting stem at base to check vascular discoloration
differential_diagnosis: Can be easily mistaken for Fusarium wilt

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne pathogen infecting through roots
Extended wet or overcast weather, waterlogging, late-maturing crops, cooler weather
disease_development_and_spread: Infects plants at seedling stage and grows continuously with plant; first symptoms appear 90-100 DAS at squaring/boll formation
severity_and_yield_loss: Plants may remain barren during severe weather conditions.

cultural_management: Balanced Nitrogen application
Correcting micronutrient deficiencies
biological_management: Seed treatment with T. viride @ 10g/kg or P. fluorescens @ 10g/kg
Soil application of T. viride or P. fluorescens @ 1 kg/acre with 100 kg FYM or vermicompost

chemical_management.application_method: Seed treatment and soil drenching at base of infected plants
Soil drenching at base of infected plants

integrated_management: Seed treatment, soil application of bioagents, balanced nutrition, and soil drenching

susceptible_varieties: G. hirsutum, G. barbadense, G. herbaceum, G. arboreum
farmer_action_points: Avoid waterlogging and late irrigation that exposes crop to cooler weather
warnings_and_limitations: Restricted mainly to south zone in India

documents.causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum race-4 (FOV4)

general: Seedling damping-off, leaf wilt, chlorosis, vascular discoloration
Black streaking at the center of root limited to roots at initial flowering stage
Root decay, wilting, and death
early_symptoms: Earliest wilting symptoms on seedlings in cotyledons
advanced_symptoms: Severe plant stunting (>80%), seedling death, bare spots in field
visual_field_symptoms: Random bare spots in fields where seedlings are killed, increasing in size over years

field_identification: Look for random bare spots in fields, seedling damping-off, and black streaking in root center
diagnostic_methods: Quarantine evaluation of imported seed and soil material
differential_diagnosis: Resembles disease caused by other fungal pathogens like FOV and Rhizoctonia solani

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne and seed-borne fungus
Movement of infested seeds or soil due to tillage or furrow irrigation, farm implements
disease_development_and_spread: Fungus produces spores persisting in soil and crop residue; spread by water, implements, and contaminated acid-delinted seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: Ability to kill seedlings and cause severe stunting greater than 80%.
prevention: Do not save and replant seed from infested fields
Clean farm equipment with pressure washer and detergent
farmer_action_points: Keep constant watch on movement of cotton seeds and material
warnings_and_limitations: Biosecurity threat; extremely virulent and causes severe early-season damage in absence of nematodes
research_findings: Race 4 detected in USA (California, Texas, New Mexico, Kansas); first described in India in 1960 on G. arboreum.

documents.causal_agent: Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum (Smith) Vauterin et al. (Xcm)

general: Water-soaked, angular leaf spots restricted by veins
Dark brown necrotic spots, 'shot-hole' appearance when necrotic tissue falls away
Vein blight (main veins as black streaks)
Black arm (elongated grayish-to-black lesions on stem)
Boll rot phase (small round water-soaked spots turning sunken and brown)
early_symptoms: Tiny round to elongate lesions on cotyledons, deep green and water-soaked spots
advanced_symptoms: Defoliation, stem cankers girdling and killing seedlings, extensive boll rotting
visual_field_symptoms: Angular dark brown spots on leaves, black streaks on veins, and black lesions on stems and bolls

field_identification: Observe underside of leaves for water-soaking around angular dark brown lesions

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed and plant debrisborne bacterium; favored by wet weather
disease_development_and_spread: Occurs from seedling to boll development stages (45 to 105 DAS); four phases: seedling phase, angular leaf spot, vein blight, black arm, and boll rot
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss up to 20%; potential yield loss estimated to be 22% with max disease index of 28.8% at Dharwad, Guntur, Surat, and Akola.

biological_management: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10g/kg or Trichoderma

chemical_management.number_of_applications: 3-4 times at fortnightly intervals starting 50 DAS

integrated_management: Seed treatment with fungicides/bioagents and foliar sprays of copper oxychloride

susceptible_varieties: Bt hybrids have manifested more susceptibility to bacterial blight compared to non-Bt counterparts
farmer_action_points: Apply copper oxychloride sprays upon initial appearance of water-soaked spots
warnings_and_limitations: Resurgence observed in central and south India in Bt hybrids
research_findings: Race-18 reported as most virulent.

documents.causal_agent: Exact cause uncertain; unique strain of Agrobacterium tumefaciens reported in Texas on taproot brown scars

general: Bronze or red discoloration and wilting of leaves ("bronzing")
Rapid wilting, collapse of youngest leaves in terminal, increase in leaf temperature
Reddening of stem and fruit shed
early_symptoms: Mild bronze leaf tint, lower leaf angle (wilting), higher leaf temperature in upper canopy
advanced_symptoms: Necrosis of stem tissue or whole plants, fruit shed, plant death
visual_field_symptoms: Sporadic occurrence of plants across field showing copper top / bronze red discoloration and wilting

field_identification: Check for sporadic bronze/red discoloration, rapid wilting, and brown scars on taproots
differential_diagnosis: Resembles Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, Macrophomina root rots, nematode damage, nutrient deficiencies, and drought

causes_and_risk_factors: Daytime temperatures above 32°C for 2-3 weeks
High light intensity, high nitrogen fertilizer rates, phosphorus/sulfur/potassium deficiencies, high soil pH (>7), drought followed by rain/irrigation

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Drought followed by rain or irrigation
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: High soil pH (above 7), nutrient deficiencies (P, S, K)

disease_development_and_spread: Occurs especially during boll development stage, often appearing first at row ends or field margins
severity_and_yield_loss: Devastating losses occurred in 1998 in USA (e.g., Georgia losses valued at nearly $25 million).
susceptible_varieties: Short-season varieties of Upland and Pima cotton
farmer_action_points: Manage irrigation and nitrogen fertilization to avoid stress conditions
warnings_and_limitations: Biosecurity threat; mysterious disease with uncertain exact cause
research_findings: Reported in Midsouth and Southeast USA during hot summers of 1995, 1996, and 1998.

documents.causal_agent: Alternaria spp. including Alternaria macrospora Zimm., Alternaria alternata (Fr.) Keissler

general: Small dull and dark brown, circular or irregularly shaped spots with concentric rings
Spots with purple margins on senescing leaves
Lesions becoming gray and dry with 'shot-holed' appearance
Coalescing spots forming large burnt/blighted patches leading to defoliation
early_symptoms: Spots on cotyledons causing them to shed
advanced_symptoms: Severe defoliation, burnt/blighted leaves
visual_field_symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings starting from lower to upper leaves across canopy, associated with reddening and yellowing

field_identification: Check for dark brown to black spots with concentric rings from lower to upper leaves, wider than target leaf spots
differential_diagnosis: Similar to Stemphylium leaf spot and Target leaf spot

causes_and_risk_factors: Insufficient potassium availability either due to inadequate fertilization or drought
Late-season cotton development

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Insufficient potassium availability

disease_development_and_spread: Appears at boll formation stages; natural infection of seeds or seed inoculation results in cotyledon infection
epidemiology: Erratic in occurrence, causing severe defoliation in some years.
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 26.6% with maximum disease index 31.6% at Rahuri, Guntur, and Dharwad (Monga et al. 2013).

cultural_management: Ensure adequate potassium fertilization
integrated_management: Balanced fertilization (potassium) combined with timely fungicide sprays

susceptible_varieties: G. hirsutum, G. barbadense, interspecific hybrids, Bt hybrids
farmer_action_points: Monitor potassium levels and apply recommended fungicides during boll development
warnings_and_limitations: Bt hybrids have manifested more susceptibility to Alternaria leaf spots
research_findings: Showing increasing trend in South and Central India.

documents.causal_agent: Cercospora gossypina Cke. (perfect state: Mycosphaerella gossypina (Cke.) Atk.)

general: Reddish spots on cotyledons and early crop stages
Lesions enlarging with white to light brown center and distinct dark brown/blackish rim
Concentric zones with red color at margins, enlarging up to 10 mm
Grey center that cracks and drops down giving target board appearance in advanced stage
early_symptoms: Reddish spots on cotyledons and early leaves
advanced_symptoms: Withering of large leaf patches, ragged margins, pale withered leaves dropping
visual_field_symptoms: Concentric spots with grey cracking centers and dark margins on older leaves

field_identification: Check for circular spots with grey cracking centers and dark margins; microscopic examination of whip-like septate spores needed for exact diagnosis
diagnostic_methods: Viewing long, thin whip-like, septate spores
differential_diagnosis: Difficult to differentiate from Alternaria, Corynespora, and Myrothecium leaf spots in the field

causes_and_risk_factors: Favorable weather under wet soil conditions when plants are unthrifty

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Wet soil conditions

disease_development_and_spread: Usually affects older leaves, spreading over whole plant in favorable wet weather
severity_and_yield_loss: Considered a minor disease and not considered to be a cause of yield loss.
research_findings: Occurs only sporadically in India and is not a serious hazard.

general: Small brown to brick-red circular to irregular spots leading to large spots (~1 inch / 2 cm)
Series of concentric rings with necrotic tissue and depression at center ("target spot" symptoms)
Dark red spots 2 mm to 10 mm in size, primarily in lower canopy
early_symptoms: Small brown to brick-red circular spots appearing as early as 60-70 DAS
advanced_symptoms: Coalescing lesions, severe necrosis, premature senescence and dropping of leaves (premature defoliation)
visual_field_symptoms: Interior canopy defoliation starting from bottom and progressing upwards, with target-pattern spots on leaves and bracts

field_identification: Check for interior canopy leaf spots with concentric rings and depression, not bordered by dark band, starting at bottom
differential_diagnosis: Differentiated from Stemphylium/Alternaria by location in canopy and absence of dark border band

causes_and_risk_factors: Frequent showers/irrigation, dense crop canopy creating microclimate, high humidity
disease_development_and_spread: Spores spread through wind and rain splash; soil and partially seed-borne, overwintering in plant debris
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses 5-40% when disease occurs early in season (at bloom) causing 10-50% defoliation.
susceptible_varieties: Various cotton cultivars and Bt hybrids depending on susceptibility
farmer_action_points: Monitor lower canopy during humid weather for early target spot lesions
warnings_and_limitations: Emerging disease with increasing trend in central and southern zones
research_findings: Reported across multiple regions in India (North Maharashtra, Nagpur, Guntur).

general: Light brown to light ash color small circular to oval spots (2-10 mm) with dark brown/violet to reddish-brown margin
Conspicuous rings of pinhead size black sporodochia in concentric rings on spots (upper and lower leaf surface)
Shot-hole appearance where center drops out, heavy defoliation
early_symptoms: Small circular to oval light brown spots with dark margins
advanced_symptoms: Coalescing spots forming large patches, leaf shedding, boll lesions damaging lint making it brittle and discolored (strained yellow/light brown)
visual_field_symptoms: Spots with concentric black fungal fruiting bodies (sporodochia) on leaves and bolls

field_identification: Check for light ash spots with dark margins and concentric rings of black sporodochia

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed-borne pathogen; favored by prolonged rainfall and humidity
disease_development_and_spread: Seed-borne; occurs all over India, severe in wet conditions
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 29.2% with maximum disease index 22.5% at Khandwa (Monga et al. 2013); losses estimated at 15% with 37% disease intensity.
susceptible_varieties: G. hirsutum and G. barbadense are more severely attacked than other species
farmer_action_points: Inspect seeds and plants during prolonged wet periods
warnings_and_limitations: Prevalent and severe in Madhya Pradesh (Khandwa)

documents.causal_agent: Colletotrichum gossypii Southw. (perfect stage: Glomerella gossypii), Colletotrichum capsici (Syd.) Butl. & Bisby

general: Reddish brown or dark brown lesions just below ground level on seedlings
Small circular sunken reddish to brown spots on leaf margins or near tips (5-10 mm)
Stem canker spots (small reddish/brown with depression in center turning black)
Reddish-brown to purplish-brown spots on bolls with depressed center, turning black with reddish margin
early_symptoms: Spots on cotyledons with irregular necrotic margins; lesions on hypocotyl causing seedling collapse
advanced_symptoms: Defoliation, salmon-pink conidial masses on spots in moist weather, internal boll lint discoloration (compact, discolored pinkish-brown)
visual_field_symptoms: Sunken reddish-brown leaf spots, stem cankers, and bolls with pink spore masses

field_identification: Check for sunken reddish-brown leaf spots near margins, stem cankers, and salmon-pink spore masses on bolls

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed infestation; favored by humid microclimate and irrigation
disease_development_and_spread: Affects plant from 20 DAS to boll maturation; seed-borne origin
severity_and_yield_loss: Losses have decreased to negligible proportions; occasionally noticed in southern and central parts of India.
farmer_action_points: Examine seedlings and bolls for sunken spots and pink spore masses

general: Numerous circular light brown spots on lower leaves (0.5-2.5 mm)
Spots turning ashy in center with dark purple ring around them
Tissue in center drops down leaving holes ('shot-holes')
early_symptoms: Circular light brown spots on lower leaves
advanced_symptoms: Early defoliation when disease is severe
visual_field_symptoms: Small spots with ashy centers and purple rings on lower leaves, causing drop-out holes

field_identification: Check lower leaves for small circular light brown spots with purple rings and ashy centers

causes_and_risk_factors: Pathogen overwinters on diseased plant debris, particularly dead leaves during off-season
disease_development_and_spread: Occurs sporadically on lower leaves
severity_and_yield_loss: Does not cause any noticeable loss in yield and is considered a minor disease.

cultural_management: Remove or destroy crop debris and dead leaves

susceptible_varieties: All four cultivated species of Gossypium including tree cotton
farmer_action_points: Clear off-season crop debris
research_findings: Observed in cotton-growing areas in India, especially Dharwad region of Karnataka.

documents.causal_agent: Ascochyta gossypii Woron. (perfect stage: Phoma exigua)

general: White to light brown circular lesions approaching 2 mm (<0.1 in) enlarging into irregular necrotic spots
Narrow dark border on necrotic margins with target-like appearance
Elongated canker spots with reddish-purple to black or ash gray on stem
Rough circular lesions on bolls following boll rotting
early_symptoms: Lesions on cotyledons and leaves in 3-8 week old plants (seedling disease)
advanced_symptoms: Death of vital parts from stem cankers, partial defoliation
visual_field_symptoms: Light brown circular spots with dark borders, black fruiting structures, and stem cankers during continuous rainy periods

field_identification: Check for light brown circular spots with dark borders, shot holes, and small black fruiting structures on older lesions
differential_diagnosis: Can easily be confused with other fungal leaf blights at early stage

causes_and_risk_factors: Continuous rainy periods; wide host range serving as collateral host
disease_development_and_spread: Appears at seedling to vegetative stages (20-60 DAS); starts on lower leaves and progresses upwards
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss is rarely reported; prolonged rains may hinder plant stand.
farmer_action_points: Monitor crop during continuous rainy periods in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka

general: Irregular, angular, pale translucent spots (1-10 mm, usually 3-4 mm) restricted by major leaf veinlets ('areolae')
Frosty or mildew growth consisting of conidiophores on undersurface and subsequently upper surface
Yellowish-brown leaves as infection progresses, necrotic lesions resembling bacterial blight
early_symptoms: Angular pale translucent spots restricted by veinlets on lower to middle canopy leaves
advanced_symptoms: Premature defoliation in severe cases
visual_field_symptoms: Angular spots with white powdery/frosty fungal growth on underside of lower to middle leaves at maturity

field_identification: Check for angular spots restricted by veins with white powdery growth on leaf underside (no other common cotton disease has white powdery growth on leaf underside)
differential_diagnosis: Can easily be confused with bacterial leaf blight at an early stage

causes_and_risk_factors: Survives on infected dead leaves, perennial cotton, volunteer plants, and overlapping crops

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Low-lying moist situations

disease_development_and_spread: Appears at vegetative to boll formation stages (60-120 DAS), starting from lower to middle canopy when plants reach maturity
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 25.6-46.6% at Dharwad, Guntur, and Nanded (Monga et al. 2013).

integrated_management: Foliar sprays of recommended fungicides

susceptible_varieties: Majority of released Bt hybrids fall in moderately susceptible to highly susceptible category; G. arboreum, G. herbaceum, G. hirsutum
prevention: Sanitation of infected dead leaves and volunteer plants
farmer_action_points: Inspect lower leaves for angular spots with white powdery growth and apply fungicides
warnings_and_limitations: Assumed to be serious in central and southern zones
research_findings: Showed increased incidence from 2008 to 2011 with PDI from 11.5 to 32.2%.

general: Rusty light to brown spots on older leaves leading to premature defoliation
Uredial sori as small (1-3 mm) pinkish-brown spots coalescing into larger patches
Yellowish-brown uredia on both leaf surfaces (primary deeply immersed on upper surface, secondary shallowly seated on lower surface)
Oval to circular uredia on pedicels and branches
early_symptoms: Rusty light to brown spots on older leaves during dry season
advanced_symptoms: Heavy defoliation, decrease in photosynthetic area
visual_field_symptoms: Rusty spots with yellowish-brown uredia on older leaves during dry season (December-March)

field_identification: Check older leaves for rusty light-brown spots and yellowish-brown uredia on both leaf surfaces in dry season

causes_and_risk_factors: Favored by cooler temperatures; appears late in season after onset of senescence or in dry season (December-March)
disease_development_and_spread: Appears at flowering to boll formation stages (120-180 DAS); only uredial stage occurs in India
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 21.7% with max disease index of 32.8% at Dharwad; avoidable loss estimated to be 21.7% in Bunny Bt and 34.05% in RCH 2 BG II.

integrated_management: Foliar sprays of Sulphur or Propiconazole

farmer_action_points: Monitor late-sown and prolonged irrigated crops during winter months for rust pustules
warnings_and_limitations: Important problem in southern zone, causing significant yield losses when appearing early
research_findings: Severe incidence noted from 2009 to 2012 in northern Karnataka.

general: Small brown and/or black colored dots on bolls enlarging to cover entire bolls
Growth of fungi and mycelia on infected bolls
Rotting of pericarp, seeds, and lint; premature opening of bolls or bolls never bursting and falling off prematurely
early_symptoms: Small brown or black colored dots on bolls during boll maturity and bursting stages
advanced_symptoms: Complete boll rotting, fiber quality affected, premature defoliation of bolls
visual_field_symptoms: Bolls covered with fungal mycelia and dark spots, rotting prematurely

field_identification: Check for discolored bolls with fungal growth, spots, and rotting during boll maturity stages

causes_and_risk_factors: Continuous cloudy weather, rain showers, warm weather, high relative humidity, insect-pest damage
disease_development_and_spread: Occurs during boll maturity and bursting stages (120-180 DAS); involves ~170 organisms in boll rot complex
severity_and_yield_loss: Productivity losses up to 20-30%.

cultural_management: Avoid water stagnation
integrated_management: Foliar sprays of copper-based fungicides

farmer_action_points: Monitor bolls during humid and rainy weather for rotting spots
warnings_and_limitations: Part of complex boll rot problem impacting lint production and quality

general: Early disease diagnosis complicated as outer surface of boll seems healthy
Immature diseased locule attributed to 'hard lock' having rotted seeds with brown dense lint
Partially opened bolls that drop or do not open properly
Immature seeds, fibers, and lint appearing discolored (light yellow, pink-red to brown) with slimy presence, swollen and rotted seeds
early_symptoms: Minute black spots as indicators of piercing-sucking insect feeding signs on carpel layer
advanced_symptoms: Severe necrosis and rot of flowering buds, young bolls, and seeds within older bolls, headlocks formed
visual_field_symptoms: Bolls appearing healthy outside but upon cross-sectioning show discolored rotted locules, slime, and hard lock

field_identification: Cross-section or open bolls to inspect locules and seeds for internal rotting, sliminess, and discolored lint without external symptoms
diagnostic_methods: Cross-sectioning bolls

causes_and_risk_factors: Invasion of developing ovary via wounds associated with insect feeding (stink bugs, hoppers, bugs) and drizzling rains during first 3 weeks of boll development

other_conditions: Piercing-sucking bug/insect infestation during bud and boll development

disease_development_and_spread: Invades via insect-feeding wounds in first 3 weeks of boll development; opportunistic bacteria (Enterobacteriaceae) and endophytic fungi
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes 10-15% yield loss in USA and 20% in China; overall boll rot causes 20-30% loss.

cultural_management: Control piercing-sucking insect vectors
integrated_management: Monitor insect populations during bud and boll development

prevention: Control sucking pests during the first 3 weeks of boll development
farmer_action_points: Cut open green bolls to check for internal slimy rot and hard locks
warnings_and_limitations: Emerging disease in central and south cotton-growing zones; difficult to diagnose without opening bolls
research_findings: Erwinia aroideae and Pantoea ananatis associated with cotton boll rot.

documents.causal_agent: Abiotic environmental factors (waterlogging, soil saturation, high temperature, bright sunshine, poor root growth)

general: Plant starts wilting from top once water stagnation takes place in root zone
Within a few days all leaves drop off while bolls remain attached
Bolls may forcefully open just prior to harvest but will not ripen fully (poor quantity and unmarketable quality)
Spreads like wildfire covering whole field within a few hours
early_symptoms: Leaves start wilting from top to bottom within a few hours
advanced_symptoms: Leaf drop, unripened open bolls
visual_field_symptoms: Large-scale rapid wilting of canopy with leaves dropping off and bolls remaining attached, roots and stem appearing healthy inside

field_identification: Check root and stem by cross-opening (appearing healthy without fungal growth) combined with rapid top-down wilting after waterlogging/rain
diagnostic_methods: Cross-opening roots and stem to check for absence of fungi

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil saturation / water logging
Rapid growth rate at grand growth stage (high transpiration and photosynthesis)
Bright sunshine and hot air temperature (high O2 requirement in roots with limited O2 in waterlogged soil)
Clayey soils, soil hard pan/compactness, low organic carbon, early irrigation, heavy boll load

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Sudden rain followed by water stagnation, heavy irrigation
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Clayey soils, poorly drained sandy soils, soil hard pan/compactness, low organic carbon

disease_development_and_spread: Occurs from flowering onwards; lack of oxygen leads to death of roots and root hairs, breaking soil-plant-atmosphere continuum
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes havoc and large-scale wilting in Bt fields across Central, South, and North zones, prominent in early maturing high-yielding Bt hybrids.

cultural_management: Avoid water stagnation and drought stress
Improve drainage in clayey soils

chemical_management.timing: Immediately after appearance of wilting symptoms
Immediately after appearance of wilting symptoms
Immediately after appearance of wilting symptoms on affected plants

integrated_management: Avoid water stagnation, foliar spray of Cobalt chloride or sodium benzoate, and drenching of copper oxychloride + urea

susceptible_varieties: Early maturing and high-yielding Bt hybrids
prevention: Ensure proper field drainage to prevent waterlogging
farmer_action_points: Act within 24-48 hours of wilting symptom onset with recommended sprays and drenching
warnings_and_limitations: Can destroy whole field within a few hours

documents.document_id: cotton__red leaf or leaf reddening complex
documents.disease_name: Red Leaf or Leaf Reddening Complex
documents.causal_agent: Abiotic stresses (nitrogen deficiency, water stagnation, high soil moisture, magnesium deficiency, cloudy weather, low night temperature, drought followed by rain/irrigation)

general: Initial symptoms appear on fully expanded leaves where area between veins in upper part becomes raised
Leaf margin becomes yellow and turns into red pigmentation covering whole leaf
Reddening progresses to other leaves and stem
Shedding of leaf and bolls due to poor plant growth
early_symptoms: Raised area between veins on fully expanded leaves, margin yellowing
advanced_symptoms: Whole leaf red pigmentation, leaf and boll shedding
visual_field_symptoms: Plants with red pigmented leaves during boll development and maturity stages

field_identification: Observe above-ground plant parts for leaf margin yellowing turning into red pigmentation during boll development

causes_and_risk_factors: Nitrogen deficiency, water stagnation, high soil moisture, magnesium deficiency, cloudy weather, low night temperature
Drought followed by rain/irrigation, high wind velocity, high solar radiation, soil with poor capacity to supply nitrogen and phosphorus

favorable_conditions.temperature: Low night temperature, high solar radiation
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Water stagnation, high soil moisture, drought followed by rain/irrigation
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Soil with poor capacity to supply nitrogen and phosphorus

disease_development_and_spread: Appears during boll development and becomes severe at boll maturity
severity_and_yield_loss: Emerged as a serious problem in various cotton-growing regions of Indian subcontinents.

cultural_management: Correct nitrogen and magnesium deficiencies
Manage soil moisture and avoid water stagnation

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: Magnesium sulphate (MgSO4) + Urea + Zinc Sulphate + Boron
chemical_management.timing: 90 days old crop, twice at 15 day intervals, followed by 2% DAP

integrated_management: Foliar nutrition sprays of MgSO4, urea, zinc sulfate, boron, and DAP

farmer_action_points: Apply recommended nutrient foliar sprays at 90 days crop stage

documents.document_id: cucurbitaceous crops__alternaria leaf spot or alternaria blight
documents.disease_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot or Alternaria Blight

general: Small circular tan spots 1-2 mm in diameter on the upper surface of older or crown leaves surrounded by a yellow halo.
Lesions on the lower leaf surface tend to be more diffused.
Spots coalesce to form large lesions more than 10 mm in diameter showing a target-like pattern of concentric rings.
early_symptoms: Small circular tan spots 1-2 mm in diameter on older or crown leaves.
advanced_symptoms: Severe leaf drop due to concentric rings on lesions.
Dark sunken brown spots initiate disease on fruits, later developing dark powdery lesions.
Fruits turn brown, reduce in size, then turn black and mummified.
visual_field_symptoms: Defoliation of vines leading to reduction in fruit yield, size, and quality.
Partial defoliation causing fruit sunscald and premature ripening.

field_identification: Target-like pattern of rings on leaf lesions.
Dark sunken brown spots on fruits.

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed- and soilborne nature.
Overwinters as dormant mycelium in crop debris and weeds.

other_conditions: Warm and dry conditions help conidia survive for several months.

disease_development_and_spread: Conidia produced in spring act as primary inoculum, carried by wind and splashing water.
Infection to symptom appearance takes 3 to 12 days.
Young plants less than a month old and fruit-bearing plants (70-75 days old) are more prone.
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes defoliation, reduction in fruit yield, size, and quality.

cultural_management: Follow a 3-year crop rotation with noncucurbitaceous crop.
Use disease-free seeds.
Grow resistant varieties/hybrids.
Sanitation practices such as cleaning up crop debris and destroying volunteer cucurbit plants and weeds.

chemical_management.timing: As soon as the disease appears

general: Talc-like (white fluffy) colonies or circular patches on the under surface of leaves.
Patches coalesce, become yellow and necrotic, and leaves die quickly in severe infections.
early_symptoms: First appears on older leaves.
advanced_symptoms: Extensive premature defoliation of older leaves.
Stunted and distorted plant parts.
visual_field_symptoms: Powdery mass on leaves decreases photosynthetic rate, plant growth, and yields.

field_identification: White powdery fungal growth on leaves, stems, and fruit.

causes_and_risk_factors: Vigorous plant growth and moderate temperature.
Densely planted fields.

other_conditions: Intensive dew on leaf surfaces enhances severity.

disease_development_and_spread: Conidia produced profusely in white powdery mycelium and spread quickly through wind.
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes yield losses of 30%–50%.

cultural_management: Monitor crops closely.
Grow resistant/tolerant varieties.
Follow field sanitation.
biological_management: Ampelomyces quisqualis Ces. (fungal spores that parasitize and destroy powdery mildew).
Bacillus subtilis.
Sporothrix flocculosa (syn. Pseudozyma flocculosa).

chemical_management.timing: At interval of 7-10 days with early symptoms
At interval of 7-10 days with early symptoms

chemical_management.application_method: Nutrient solution (fertigation) or foliar spray of chlorite mica clay
chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Significantly delayed and reduced disease incidence / suppression of powdery mildew

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Cucumber and melon varieties with genetic resistance
warnings_and_limitations: Powdery mildew fungi can develop resistance to specific fungicides.

general: Pale green areas on the upper surface of leaves that change to bright yellow angular or rectangular spots delimited by leaf veins.
Lesions expand, coalesce, and tissues turn necrotic and brown.
early_symptoms: Pale green areas on upper leaf surface.
advanced_symptoms: Shriveling and death of large areas of leaf surface giving a scorched appearance.
Lower surface shows water-soaked, slightly sunken lesions with profuse light to dark gray or purple sporulation.
visual_field_symptoms: Field has a brown and brittle look as lesions expand.

field_identification: Angular leaf spots delimited by veins with dark purplish gray sporulation on the underside of leaves.
differential_diagnosis: Symptoms on watermelon and cantaloupe are not as distinctive and mostly mistaken for anthracnose, target spot, Alternaria leaf spot, or gummy stem blight.

causes_and_risk_factors: High humidity, fog, and heavy dew.
disease_development_and_spread: Overwinters on infected cucurbit plants in areas without hard frost.
Sporangia spread via wind currents or rain splashes.
Germinate and directly infect leaves within an hour.
severity_and_yield_loss: Kills the plant quickly through rapid defoliation.

cultural_management: Grow resistant/tolerant varieties.
Monitor crops.
Trellis vining cultivars so leaves dry quickly.
Increase plant spacing or grow in greenhouses.
Early planting.
Avoid excess overhead irrigation and apply during late morning.
biological_management: Bacillus subtilis (wettable powder formulation)

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Resistant varieties especially cucumber (though new races reduce resistance)
warnings_and_limitations: No organic-approved fungicides or biofungicides prevent or control cucurbit downy mildew.

general: Water-soaked lesions on leaves turning yellowish circular spots, then brown to black.
Irregular spots on watermelon foliage turning dark brown or black; brown spots on cucumber and muskmelon.
Long dark spots develop on stems; stem lesions on muskmelon can girdle and cause wilting.
early_symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves.
advanced_symptoms: Roughly circular, sunken, water-soaked spots with dark borders on mature fruits (6-13 mm diameter, 6 mm deep on watermelon).
Black fruiting structures (acervuli) formed within lesions.
Black stromata with gelatinous mass of salmon pink spores.
visual_field_symptoms: Vine defoliation, fruit decline, and death of plant.

field_identification: Cankers lined with characteristic salmon pink color on fruits and stems.

causes_and_risk_factors: Humid and moist weather conditions.

other_conditions: Requires water to liberate conidia from sticky covering.

disease_development_and_spread: Overwinters on infected residue and cucurbit seeds.
Releases conidia in spring under humid conditions.
severity_and_yield_loss: Huge losses in storage or shipment if infected fruits are packed.

cultural_management: Grow resistant/tolerant varieties.
Obtain clean seed from production areas without anthracnose problems.
Monitor crops closely.
Clean up crop debris and wild hosts.
Deep plowing immediately after final harvest.
Long crop rotation with noncucurbit crops.
Ensure proper drainage.
biological_management: Bacillus subtilis strain QST713
Endophytic Streptomyces sp. strain MBCu-56

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Cultivars with varying levels of resistance offered by public institutes and seed companies
warnings_and_limitations: Fungicide applications generally are not required within 2-3 weeks of final harvest.

general: Numerous water-soaked spots on leaves and runners turning gray to white, angular with yellow margins.
Center of leaf spots drops out giving irregular-shaped holes.
Oblong lesions on stem and petiole covered with dark-green velvety mold.
advanced_symptoms: Fruit spots ooze gummy substance, invaded by secondary rotting bacteria causing foul smell.

field_identification: Gummy substance oozing from fruit spots, dark-green velvety mold on stem and petiole lesions.
differential_diagnosis: Lesions on fruit are often confused with Anthracnose.

causes_and_risk_factors: Low night temperature, fog, and low light intensity.

other_conditions: Low night temperature, fog, and low light intensity.

disease_development_and_spread: Overwinters on crop debris and seed.
Spores blown long distances in moist air, spread by insects, implements, and worker clothing.

cultural_management: Grow resistant cultivars.
Harvest seed from disease-free plants.
Remove plant debris and fruits after harvest.
Crop rotation with noncucurbitaceous crops.
Avoid low-lying, shaded areas prone to heavy fogs and dews.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation.

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: Photodynamic dyes (bengal rose, toluidine blue, methylene blue)
