general: Dark spots seen first on older leaves.
Circular to irregular spots with pale or light centers and dark margins.
advanced_symptoms: Lesions expand, coalesce, and give a blighted appearance.
visual_field_symptoms: Defoliation occurs in severe cases, reducing fruit size and quality.

field_identification: Circular to irregular leaf spots with pale centers and dark margins on older leaves.

causes_and_risk_factors: Survives on infested crop debris and weeds between crops.
disease_development_and_spread: Spores spread readily by wind currents, splashing rain, and irrigation water.
severity_and_yield_loss: Economic losses are rarely severe.

cultural_management: Crop rotation with noncucurbitaceous crops.
Avoid overhead irrigation and irrigation in the morning hours.
Sanitation by removing old diseased crop residues and cucurbitaceous weeds.
Deep plowing immediately after final harvest.

general: Small, circular tan spots on leaves, sometimes with yellow halo.
Water-soaked reddish-brown spots on midveins and petioles with a ringed appearance.
early_symptoms: Infection often begins at leaf margins.
advanced_symptoms: Stem lesions: oblong, water-soaked brown lesions that enlarge and girdle main stem.
Stems split open, oozing characteristic red or brown gummy fluid from cankers.
Tiny black pimple-like fruiting bodies on stem or nodes.
Fruit (black rot): pale brown then bleached patches, reddish gum oozing from cracks, pycnidia, irregular water-soaked spots turning dark brown.
visual_field_symptoms: Wilting and death of plants (crown rot).

field_identification: Red or brown gummy fluid oozing from stem cankers.
differential_diagnosis: May be confused with downy mildew, but leaf spots are larger.

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted through seed, soil, and air.
disease_development_and_spread: Survives on crop residue and in soil for 2 years without a host.
severity_and_yield_loss: Fruits can rot within 2-3 days after infection.

cultural_management: Procure disease-free seeds from reliable sources.
Crop rotation with nonhost crops.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Remove and destroy infected fruits and vines at the end of the season.
Avoid injury to fruit before or during harvest.
biological_management: Bacillus subtilis (Serenade 10WP at 4.5 kg/ha)

chemical_management.timing: As soon as the disease is noticed

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Effectively managed disease and reduced fungicide use
Effectively managed disease and reduced fungicide use

integrated_management: Combined use of green manure with Melcast-scheduled fungicide application, chlorothalonil, B. subtilis, and pyraclostrobin plus boscalid.

general: Bleached appearance on infected leaves and stems near crown, turning brown to black later.
Black streaks within the pith on cutting open the collar region.
advanced_symptoms: Black sclerotia visible on removal of epidermis of stem.
visual_field_symptoms: Affected plants die under hot and dry weather conditions.

field_identification: Black sclerotia under stem epidermis and black streaks in the pith.
differential_diagnosis: Symptoms are very similar to gummy stem blight, but appear late in the season.

causes_and_risk_factors: Hot climate.

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Saline soils

disease_development_and_spread: Roots become infected first, then fungus invades plant crown.
Persists in soil and crop residue as microsclerotia for 3–12 years.

cultural_management: Grafting susceptible scions onto resistant cucurbit rootstock.
Long-term crop rotation with nonhost crops.
Destroy infected plant debris at the end of growing season.
Management of saline soils.

documents.causal_agent: Pythium spp., Rhizoctonia spp., and Fusarium spp.

general: Preemergence damping-off: rotting of seed inside seed coat.
Radicle and cotyledon turn brown and soft.
early_symptoms: Initial postemergence symptoms: yellow to dark brown, water-soaked lesions on root and hypocotyl tissues.
advanced_symptoms: Hypocotyl tissues shrivel, roots decay further, seedlings topple down or wilt and collapse.
Roots have watery gray appearance, particularly fine feeder roots.

causes_and_risk_factors: Cool temperatures, high soil moisture, and poor aeration.

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Poor aeration

cultural_management: Ensure proper drainage and avoid overwatering.
Field sanitation after final harvest.
Crop rotation with noncucurbitaceous crops.
biological_management: Combined application of organic amendments and microbial biocontrol agents

general: Loss of turgor pressure of vines; wilting starts on older leaves and advances to young foliage.
Temporary wilting during peak heat periods, reviving at night.
Vascular browning, gummosis, and tylosis in xylem vessels.
early_symptoms: Hypocotyl rot or toppling down at soil line in seedlings.
advanced_symptoms: Whole plant may wilt and die within a few days.
White-to-pink fungal growth on surface of dead tissues in wet weather.
visual_field_symptoms: Wilt symptoms develop on one or few lateral vines initially.

field_identification: Vascular browning and temporary wilting during peak heat periods.

causes_and_risk_factors: High nitrogen (ammoniacal form), less than 25% soil moisture, light, sandy, and slightly acidic soils (pH 5-5.5).

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Light, sandy, and slightly acidic soils (pH 5-5.5), less than 25% soil moisture

disease_development_and_spread: Fungi invade roots and progress into stems.
Survives in old infected plant debris, other host plants, seed, or soil.
Monocyclic (does not spread plant to plant during season); spread within field via infested soil, across fields via infected equipment and plants.

cultural_management: Procure disease-free seeds and seedlings from reliable sources.
Grow resistant varieties/hybrids.
Rotate with noncucurbitaceous crops such as garlic, radish, onion, and beetroot.
Soil solarization.
Use other cucurbit species resistant to Fusarium wilt as rootstocks for grafting (e.g., Lagenaria siceraria and Cucurbita moschata × C. maxima hybrids).
Destroy plant debris and weeds after crop harvest.
biological_management: Bacillus subtilis (strain-B006 powder)
Gliocladium spp., Trichoderma spp., and Pseudomonas spp.
Nonpathogenic strains of F. oxysporum
Cover crops such as hairy vetch
integrated_management: Integration of soil amendments, biocontrol agents, and resistant rootstocks.

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Resistant rootstocks: Lagenaria siceraria and Cucurbita moschata × Cucurbita maxima hybrids
warnings_and_limitations: No complete resistance to all races available in any commercial watermelon lines.

documents.document_id: cucurbitaceous crops__vine decline or crown blight

general: Stunting of young plants or severe yellowing of foliage.
Chlorosis of lower older leaves that later wilt and collapse.
advanced_symptoms: Roots appear as tan to red-brown lesions that expand, resulting in death of small feeder roots.
Root system may rot and plant collapse.
visual_field_symptoms: Collapse of vine reduces fruit size, number, quality, or causes sunburn symptoms due to lack of foliage.

field_identification: Minute black, spherical, and erumpent perithecia at perithecial openings on entire root along with brown rot lesions.

disease_development_and_spread: Perithecia rupture and ascospores fall into soil (soilborne).
Root infection occurs about 57 days after planting in spring crop, or within 9 days in late-spring/fall crop.

cultural_management: Preplant soil fumigation with methyl bromide, chloropicrin, 1,3-dichloropropene, or metam sodium.
Sanitize field by destroying infected roots immediately after final harvest.
Apply metam sodium in sick field immediately after harvest.
Use grafted melons on resistant squash (Cucurbita spp.) or bottle gourd (Lagenaria spp.) rootstocks.
Long crop rotation with noncucurbitaceous crops.
Avoid overirrigation and ensure proper drainage.
biological_management: Cover crops such as canola, winter rape, and mustards

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Resistant squash (Cucurbita spp.) or bottle gourd (Lagenaria spp.) rootstocks

documents.disease_name: Phytophthora Blight or Phytophthora Crown and Root Rot
documents.causal_agent: Phytophthora capsici, Phytophthora drechsleri, and Phytophthora parasitica

general: Pre- and postemergence damping-off, stem and vine blight, wilting of young shoots and leaves, wilting and collapse of whole foliage or fruit rot.
early_symptoms: Early fruit symptoms: large, water-soaked or slightly sunken, circular lesions that enlarge and cover fruit with white mold.
advanced_symptoms: Mature plants wilt suddenly; upon uprooting, tan to brown rotted root system with fine feeder roots breaking off.
Stem and leaf petiole lesions are light to dark brown, water soaked, soft, and irregular, gradually rotting and becoming papery.
visual_field_symptoms: Total loss of the crop.

field_identification: White mold on fruit and papery stem/petiole lesions.

causes_and_risk_factors: Poor drainage, heavy textured soils, low-lying damp areas.

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Poor drainage, high moisture

disease_development_and_spread: Initial inoculum consists of oospores surviving as dormant propagules in soil.
Zoospores infect crown and root tissues.
Sporangia in white mold dispersed by wind and rain.
severity_and_yield_loss: May result in total loss of the crop.

cultural_management: Do not select low-lying damp area or poor draining and heavy textured soils.
Long crop rotation with nonsusceptible host crops.
Avoid overirrigation and ensure proper drainage.
Carefully discard crop debris after harvest.
Proper trellising of vines.
Raise bush type cucurbits on dome-shaped ridges or raised beds.
Do not harvest seeds from infested fruits.

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Protect seedlings up to 5 weeks of transplanting
Combined application with seed treatment reduces damage

general: Small, water-soaked lesions on leaves that later enlarge; angular shape as they encounter veins.
Affected tissues dry and fall, leaving torn irregular-shaped holes in leaves.
early_symptoms: Small, water-soaked lesions on leaves.
advanced_symptoms: Leaves turn yellow, growing tips of vines become water-soaked and yellow and growth ceases.
Fruit infection: small circular spots with yellow halo, turning dull white with dry cracks.
visual_field_symptoms: White bacterial ooze on underside of lesions under very humid conditions, drying to thin white crust.

field_identification: Angular leaf lesions with torn irregular holes and white bacterial crust on underside.

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed- and soilborne nature; survives as vegetative cells in seed, soil, plant debris, or weeds.
disease_development_and_spread: Disseminated by splashing rain, irrigation water, soil, insects, farm tools, and field workers.
Infection through natural openings and wounds.
severity_and_yield_loss: Reduction in fruit number, fruit yield, and quality.

cultural_management: Use only disease-free seeds.
3-year or longer crop rotation with noncucurbitaceous crops.
Maintain field sanitation.
Do not work in crop when it is wet.
Deep plowing and soil solarization in summer months.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Avoid injury during intercultural operations.
Manage nighttime humidity (80%–90%) with dehumidifiers under protected structures.
biological_management: Pentaphage (lysate of virulent strain of P. syringae)
Isolate of L33 strain of Pseudomonas geniculata

general: Small brown spots on cotyledons.
Necrotic spots on leaves: small water-soaked or greasy patches on underside, indefinite yellow patches on upper side turning brown, round to angular with translucent centers and yellow halo.
early_symptoms: Small brown spots on cotyledons.
advanced_symptoms: Fruit symptoms: water-soaked, sunken, cracked areas with light-brown exudates, distinct sinking, rind cracking, viscous liquid drops of yellowish-brown color in damp weather.
visual_field_symptoms: Rotting of flesh and contamination of seed if infection progresses into seed cavity.

field_identification: Necrotic leaf spots with translucent centers and yellow halo where necrotic areas do not fall out.

causes_and_risk_factors: Warm and humid conditions.
disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by seed, infected crop residue, rain splash, and infected tools.
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses may exceed 50% under humid/moist conditions.

cultural_management: Management practices similar to angular leaf spot.

warnings_and_limitations: No reports of biological control for bacterial spot of cucurbits.

general: Greasy, water-soaked lesions on undersurface of cotyledons extending along veins and stems to true leaves.
early_symptoms: Elongated and dark to reddish-brown lesions on cotyledon veins.
advanced_symptoms: Fruit symptoms: small, irregular, olive-colored, water-soaked spots just prior to harvest maturity, enlarging rapidly, turning reddish brown with cracks, white bacterial ooze under high humidity.
visual_field_symptoms: Seedling collapse in damping-off fashion in severe cases.

field_identification: Olive-colored water-soaked spots on fruits turning reddish brown with cracks and white bacterial ooze.
differential_diagnosis: Can be confused with abiotic stresses; water congestion on leaves does not persist till daytime.

causes_and_risk_factors: Infected seeds/seedlings as primary source of inoculum.
disease_development_and_spread: Spreads by mechanical means, rain, or sprinklers.

cultural_management: Procure seeds from disease-free mother fruits.
Controlled in protected structures by maintaining low temperature and low humidity.
Long crop rotations.
Avoid overhead irrigation and do not work in fields while foliage is wet.
Observe for infection regularly, destroy affected seedlings immediately, or burn crop under severe infection.

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Dark-colored watermelon fruits are least susceptible
susceptible_varieties: Light-green watermelon fruits are highly susceptible; striped fruits are moderately susceptible
warnings_and_limitations: Seed treatments including thermotherapy, NaOCl, fermentation, HCl, and peroxyacetic acid can adversely affect seed physiology.

general: External symptoms usually absent, misshapen fruits in few severely affected melons.
Brown, dry, and hard necrosis of rind rarely extending into flesh.
Corky layers appear between outer rind and edible fruit tissues in cross section.
visual_field_symptoms: Fruits look good and marketable externally; unmarketable only when sliced.

field_identification: Internal brown, dry, hard necrosis of the rind with corky layers visible upon slicing.

causes_and_risk_factors: Caused by bacteria naturally present in watermelon fruits.

cultural_management: Avoid planting melons in fields where rind necrosis has been encountered.

warnings_and_limitations: There is no chemical treatment for this disease and varietal resistance is controversial.

general: Mottled mosaic leaf pattern of alternate light-green and dark-green patches with edges curling downward on young leaves.
Yellow-colored mottling, leaf distortion, stunted plant growth due to shortening of stem internodes.
Older leaves develop chlorotic areas turning necrotic along margins.
early_symptoms: Mottled mosaic leaf pattern on young leaves of ~6-week-old plants.
advanced_symptoms: Stem end portion of infected fruits mottled with yellowish-green and dark-green spots, forming wartlike raised dark spots (distorted fruit).
Smooth gray-white color with irregular green areas ('white pickle') in later stages.
Bitter taste in cucumber fruits, soggy pickles; blotchy appearance in squash.
visual_field_symptoms: Wilting of petioles leaving older vine mostly bare; slow decline of plant health.

field_identification: Yellow-colored leaf mottling, leaf distortion, shortened internodes, and wartlike raised dark spots on fruits.
diagnostic_methods: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted through aphid vectors (Aphis gossypii, Myzus persicae), seeds, and weed hosts.

other_conditions: Overwinters in perennial weed sources attractive to aphids in spring.

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by aphid vectors and mechanical sap transmission via hands/clothes of workers.

cultural_management: Grow resistant varieties.
Use virus-indexed seeds and seedlings.
Carefully monitor and remove plants with symptoms early.
Grow taller nonsusceptible barrier crops like corn.
Remove all weeds and volunteer cucurbit crop plants.
Avoid planting cucurbits consecutively in close proximity.
Destroy plant debris promptly after harvest.
Long crop rotations with noncucurbitaceous crops.
Use superreflective plastic mulch, floating row covers, or reflective mulches.
Burn severely infected crops.
biological_management: Parasitoids (Aphidius colemani, Aphidius matricariae, Lysiphlebus fabarum, Binodoxys angelicae)

warnings_and_limitations: Managing viruses through insecticides is not a good approach because insecticides do not act fast enough to prevent aphid spread.

general: Stunting, chlorotic leaf mottling, green vein banding, and leaf distortion of infected seedlings.
Older infected plants develop distorted margins, blistering, hardening, and mild to severe dark-green mosaic pattern on leaves.
early_symptoms: Stunting, chlorotic leaf mottling, green vein banding on seedlings.
advanced_symptoms: Infected fruits have mottling on skin and become malformed or distorted.

field_identification: Dark-green mosaic pattern on leaves (may be confused with hormonal herbicide effect).
differential_diagnosis: Mosaic pattern may be confused with hormonal herbicide effect.

causes_and_risk_factors: Seedborne; spread by beetles (Acalymma and Diabrotica).
disease_development_and_spread: Spread by beetles injecting virus via saliva upon feeding, and through mechanical injury.

cultural_management: Resistant varieties, virus-indexed seeds, rouging, weed removal, crop rotation, and vector control.

warnings_and_limitations: Virus is carried within seed and cannot be eliminated by hot water or chemical treatment.

general: Blistered, deformed leaves with severe mosaic symptoms, reduction in size, and stunted plant growth.
advanced_symptoms: Melon fruits: discolored with hardening of flesh, seed deformation, and external cracks.
Pumpkin and zucchini fruits: discolored and deformed due to knobbiness.
Rockmelon fruits: poor surface netting.

field_identification: Blistered, deformed leaves with severe mosaic symptoms and knobby, discolored fruits.

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by aphid species (Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii, cowpea aphid).

other_conditions: High activity of aphids causes fast spread.

cultural_management: Resistant varieties, virus-indexed seeds, hot air/water seed treatment (C. pepo with hot air 70°C for 2 days or hot water 50°C for 60 min), rouging, barrier crops, weed removal, crop rotation, reflective mulches, vector management.

general: Characteristic mosaic symptoms: profuse mottling, puckering, and deformation of crown leaves (lower mature leaves unaffected).
Leaf distortion and blistering.
advanced_symptoms: Infected zucchini and pumpkin: lumpy, distorted fruits.
Rockmelon fruits: poor-quality surface netting.
Watermelon fruits: uneven surface or typical ring spot patterns on skin.

field_identification: Mottling, puckering, and deformation of crown leaves with ring spot patterns on watermelon skin.

causes_and_risk_factors: Spread by aphid species including green peach and melon aphids; wild and native cucurbit species act as infection reservoirs.

cultural_management: General virus management practices (resistant varieties, sanitation, vector control).

susceptible_varieties: Zucchini squash most susceptible, followed by watermelon and cucumber

general: Petunia-like appearance of diseased vines: tips of vines and proliferation of shoots around crown extend beyond general level of vines.
Shortened internodal length resulting in crowding of leaves that become rolled, blistered, and small in size with mild mosaic symptoms.
advanced_symptoms: Abnormal flower size, shape, and color resulting in mottled, misshapen small fruits.

field_identification: Petunia-like vine appearance with crowded, rolled, blistered small leaves.
differential_diagnosis: Produces less severe symptoms on cucurbit leaves and fruits than PRSV, ZYMV, and SqMV.

severity_and_yield_loss: Has little effect on fruits directly compared to leaf symptoms, though severe infections cause mottled misshapen small fruits.

cultural_management: General virus management practices.

susceptible_varieties: Cucurbita pepo, C. maxima, and C. moschata

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by nematodes (Xiphinema americanum).

Sori are oval or cylindrical, dirty grey sacs, sometimes conical at the tip, measuring 4-12 mm in length.
advanced_symptoms: Sacs rupture easily, and the interior is completely filled with spore powder.
visual_field_symptoms: Symptoms become visible only at the time of grain formation stage.

general: Severe defoliation especially during the grain-filling period
Starts as long, elliptical, gray-green lesions measuring 3-15 cm in length
early_symptoms: Infection occurs from the lower lamina, gradually extending to the upsides
advanced_symptoms: Lesions mature to tan color with targeted, darkish zones of fungal sporulation
Lesions may coalesce forming enormous blighted areas, and entire leaves may emerge as blighted
visual_field_symptoms: Extensive defoliation during the grain filling period

field_identification: Long, elliptical, gray-green to tan lesions with darkish zones of fungal sporulation

causes_and_risk_factors: High humidity coupled with low temperature and cloudy weather
Growing sorghum and maize together
disease_development_and_spread: Infection occurs from seedling to harvesting, with maximum severity seen from tasseling and six to eight weeks after on silking.

Maize yield decreases up to 0.6 t ha-1 when severity reaches more than 75%

cultural_management: Crop rotation of one to two years
Deep burying of infested maize residues before planting maize hybrids
Timely removal of overwintering infected crop residue
Application of adequate potassium in the form of potassium chloride

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Efficacy in controlling TLB both in vitro and in field conditions
Improved seed emergence and seedling vigor and reduced initial inoculum
Improved seed emergence and seedling vigor and reduced initial inoculum
Reduced initial inoculum and disease severity

integrated_management: Seed treatment with carboxin + thiram or benomyl + thiram followed by foliar application of mancozeb (0.25%) thrice at 10 days interval

general: Appears at a pre-flowering stage in 40-50 days old plants
Starts from the leaf sheath or on leaves in contact with soil and travels up to the ear
early_symptoms: Initially water-soaked and narrow purple-brown bands oriented perpendicular to long axis of leaves or leaf sheath
advanced_symptoms: Alternate bleached area or zones
visual_field_symptoms: Infected cobs bearing sclerotia

field_identification: Alternate bleached zones with narrow purple-brown bands perpendicular to the long axis

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne nature
Rice-maize cropping pattern
High crop densities

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Rainfall over 100 mm in the first two weeks of infection

disease_development_and_spread: Secondary spread is due to contact of healthy plants with infected leaves/sheaths.

Magnitude of grain loss may reach as high as 100% if the ear rot phase predominates

cultural_management: Selection of a well-drained field and planting on raised beds
Composting of hardwood on infested soil
Stripping of the second and third leaf-sheath from the ground level at the age of 35-40 days old crop
biological_management: Trichoderma spp., Gliocladium virens, and Pseudomonas fluorescens

Highly effective seed dressing fungicide with 48.7% disease control and highest yield of 64.7 q/ha over control
Very effective against R. solani and potent to give high level of disease control

integrated_management: Foliar application of carbendazim followed by Trichoderma sprays in sawdust and FYM amended field
Validamycin (0.25%) and T. viride as foliar spray

research_findings: Identified 11 QTLs for resistance to BLSB on chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 10.

general: Infected plants are chlorotic with chlorotic area including the base of the blade with transverse margin
Leaves tend to be narrower and more erect than healthy plants
A white downy mildew growth may appear on lower surfaces of infected leaves
Tassels may exhibit phyllody with no seed set
visual_field_symptoms: Chlorotic leaves with transverse margins, white downy growth underneath, and tassel phyllody

field_identification: Chlorotic leaves with defined transverse margins and white downy fungal growth on lower surfaces

causes_and_risk_factors: Plants less than one-month-old are highly susceptible
disease_development_and_spread: Polycyclic disease cycle capable of causing secondary infections throughout the growing season. Oospores overwinter in soil and plant debris.
severity_and_yield_loss: Severe losses worldwide (in tune of $25 billion)

cultural_management: Avoidance of monoculture
Removal, destruction, and burning of infected plant debris along with weeds
Rouging of infected plants in early stages
biological_management: Chytrid fungus (Gaeumannomyces spp.) added to soil to parasitize oospores (reduced systemic infection up to 58%)

research_findings: More than 5000 germplasm lines evaluated for host plant resistance.

general: Occurs after flowering stage and prior to physiological maturity
Internal decay and discoloration of stalk tissues
Rotting extends from infected roots to the stalk causing premature drying, stalk breakage, and ear dropping
advanced_symptoms: Affected plants die prematurely producing lightweight ears with poorly filled kernels
Plants easily lodge
visual_field_symptoms: Premature drying, lodging, stalk breakage, and dropped ears

field_identification: Stalk internal decay/discoloration, premature drying, and lodging during grain filling

causes_and_risk_factors: Water stress after flowering / high soil temperature
Sandy soils
Excess nitrogen fertilizers compared to potash

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy soil, moisture stress after flowering

disease_development_and_spread: Soil-borne infection pathway; fungus survives on crop residue in soil or on soil surface.
severity_and_yield_loss: Incidence varying from 5 to 40% at different parts of the country

cultural_management: Application of farmyard manure and neem cake
biological_management: Trichoderma pseudokoningii
Trichoderma harzianum
Seed treatment with T. harzianum (4 g/kg seed) along with soil application of castor or neem cake (250 kg/ha) 15 days prior to sowing

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Effectively reduced ear rot disease and fumonisins accumulation

integrated_management: Application of farmyard manure and neem cake along with Trichoderma harzianum 15–20 days before sowing with two additional irrigation at tasseling and silking stage
Integration of T. viride (drenching) with bavistin seed treatment

warnings_and_limitations: Fungicidal control of Fusarium stalk rot is not effective due to its soil-borne infection pathway.
research_findings: Identified QTLs and major genes for resistance on chromosomes 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10.

documents.causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis Shlecht. emend. Snyder and Hansen f. sp. lentis Vasud. and Srini

general: Patches of wilted plants appear in the field at seedling and adult stages
Wilting of leaves resembling water deficiency
Stunting and shrinking of plants
Curling of leaves from lower parts moving progressively up the stem
early_symptoms: Pre-emergence and post-emergence damping off
Seedling blight
Sudden drooping and drying of plants resulting in seedling death
advanced_symptoms: Dark brown discoloration in the xylem tissue of roots and stems visible upon vertical splitting
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of wilted plants in the field

field_identification: Patches of wilted plants
Dark brown discoloration of root and stem xylem tissue when split vertically
diagnostic_methods: Screening tests under field trials, greenhouses, and laboratory settings

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil contamination and plant debris
Infected seeds
Warm soil temperatures and dry soil conditions
Synergistic interaction with plant-pathogenic nematodes like Ditylenchus spp., Meloidogyne spp., and Pratylenchus spp.

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Dry soil conditions, sandy loam soil compared to clay soil, soil pH up to 7.5

disease_development_and_spread: Fungal spores germinate and elongate towards host roots in response to plant signals
Penetration via natural openings or wounds, invading root cortex, epidermis, and reaching xylem vessels
Vertical growth, multiplication, and colonization in xylem until plant wilting
Transmission through plant debris, soil contamination, and seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: May cause 5-10% yield loss, but complete crop failure can occur under favorable conditions
Yield loss ranging from 9.6% to 100% and wilt incidence ranging from 20% to 46.67%

cultural_management: Delaying sowing
Ensuring use of clean and disease-free seeds
Planting seeds at proper depth around 10-12 cm
Intercropping or mixed cropping
Deep plowing and removal of infected crop residues
Soil solarization
Chemical amendments involving manganese and zinc
Selecting early maturing cultivars or adjusting planting time
Applying manure or compost
biological_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum @ 6 g/kg seed

Use of antagonists like Pseudomonas fluorescens, Trichoderma viride, Bacillus velezensis, Streptomyces, Glomus coronatum, Gliocladium, Piriformospora indica, Sebacina vermafera, and Penicillium chrysogenum
Plant extracts of Azadirachta indica, Justicia adhatoda, Ficus religiosa, Carica papaya, Ricinus communis, Ficus benghalensis, Psidium guajava, and Tamarindus indica at concentrations above 15%

prevention: Use of clean and disease-free seeds
farmer_action_points: Select resistant varieties
Use clean seeds
Adjust sowing dates

documents.causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea Pers. ex Fr. and Botrytis fabae Sardiña

general: Dark green spots on lower foliage turning into pale tan-colored spots
Infected leaves and flowers deteriorate into rotting masses
Pods become seedless or deformed with undersized seeds
Lesions on stems are light brown or blanched, covered with gray mold, and rot at the crown
advanced_symptoms: Whole plant eventually becomes infected and dried out
visual_field_symptoms: Scattered pattern of dead plants in the field that rapidly spreads
Fuzzy spore masses and black sclerotia on infected stems

field_identification: Gray mold growth on stems, flowers, and pods
Scattered pattern of dead plants

causes_and_risk_factors: Dense crop canopy
High humidity (>95%)
Moderate temperature (15-25 °C)
High rainfall
Wet periods exceeding 10 hours
Early sowing
Overhead irrigation or waterlogging

favorable_conditions.rainfall: >20 mm for susceptible varieties, >40 mm for moderately susceptible varieties

disease_development_and_spread: Infection starts on flowers and pods
Conidia serve as sources of secondary infection dispersed through air
Survival through mycelium, sclerotia, and chlamydospores, as well as infected seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield reduction from 30% to complete failure
Yield losses of more than 50% reported in Australia

cultural_management: Crop rotation
Adjusting sowing dates
Reducing seed rate
Weed control
Optimal fertilizer use
Rotating fungicides with different modes of action
Selecting resistant cultivars
Stubble grazing or burning
Controlling volunteer plants
biological_management: Application of biocontrol agents such as Pseudomonas fluorescens, Pantoea agglomerans, Penicillium griseofulvum, Penicillium aurantiogriseum, Trichoderma hamatum, and Trichoderma harzianum

chemical_management.timing: mid-flower in early-seeded cultivars or early flower in late-seeded cultivars
chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: provided comparable efficacy to multiple applications

integrated_management: Combining foliar fungicides, seed treatments, resistant cultivars, physical treatments, and cultural methods

farmer_action_points: Use seed treatments
Practice crop rotation
Plant resistant cultivars
warnings_and_limitations: Fungicide resistance development in Botrytis cinerea poses a significant threat

general: Initial symptoms appear on upper canopy
Minute gray or light brown lesions on leaflets with pinhead-like appearance
Lesions undergo irregular enlargement and rapidly spread
Infected tissue appears light cream-colored with angular pattern
Infected stems dry up, exhibiting inverted J-shaped appearance and turning ashy white
advanced_symptoms: Significant defoliation leaving only terminal leaflets
Flower abortion and reduced seed germination rates
visual_field_symptoms: Completely blighted field appearance within 7-10 days
Field can appear as if burnt by fire

field_identification: Minute gray or light brown pinhead lesions on leaflets spreading rapidly
Inverted J-shaped ashy white stems

causes_and_risk_factors: High temperatures
Long wet periods
Cloudy weather, foggy days

other_conditions: Cloudy and foggy days (30-50 days per year)

Airborne conidia act as secondary source of inoculum
Conidia germinate within 6 hours under moisture, entering via stomata or epidermal penetration
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses of up to 62% in Bangladesh, exceeding 90% in Bihar, India
Complete crop failure under highly favorable conditions

cultural_management: Destruction of old crop residue
Crop rotation with non-host crops
Delaying sowing or early sowing on November 1
biological_management: Application of botanicals derived from Acoros calamus and Zanthoxylum armatum
Use of Trichoderma viride and Trichoderma harzianum

effective disease control and increased lentil yield

farmer_action_points: Use resistant varieties

Seed-borne infection

Spreads upwards through rain splash

Planting new lentil crops at considerable distance from previous fields
Eliminating volunteer lentils and wild vetch
Soaking infested seeds in hot water at 52 °C for 30 min

documents.causal_agent: Ascochyta pisi, Phoma medicaginis var. pinodella (A. pinodella), and Mycosphaerella pinodes (A. pinodes)

general: Purple necrotic lesions on stems, tendrils, leaves, and pods
Dark spore-producing structures
Discoloration on seeds
early_symptoms: Small purple to black spots that expand when moist
Purple-brown irregular flecks on lower leaves, stems, and tendrils under humid conditions
advanced_symptoms: Enlarged lesions that are round to oval in shape containing brown concentric rings
Blue-black appearance at lower stem areas
Stem girdling close to the soil line
Blight and leaf fall
Lesions on pods causing early pod senescence
visual_field_symptoms: Dark spore producing structures
Purple necrotic lesions on stems, tendrils, leaves, and pods
Necrotic leaf spots and stem lesions with blackening

field_identification: Small purplish-black spots on leaves enlarging to round or oval lesions with brown concentric rings
Blue-black appearance at the lower stem areas
Purple-brown irregular flecks leading to blight and leaf fall
diagnostic_methods: Observation of morphological characteristics and spore mass color on oat meal agar (OA) medium
Presence of pseudothecia for Didymella pinodes
differential_diagnosis: Didymella pinodes produces pseudothecia and light buff spore mass on OA medium
Phoma medicaginis causes more severe damage on leaves and pods and foot rot, with conidia smaller than D. pinodes and A. pisi
Ascochyta pisi has sunken, tan to light brown leaf lesions surrounded by darker brown, does not cause foot rot, has smaller black pycnidia, and produces carrot-red spore masses on OA

causes_and_risk_factors: Infected seed acting as primary source of inoculum
Infected crop residue and soil
Lack of affordable fungicides and low host resistance

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Soil-borne survival structures persisting for more than 5 years

disease_development_and_spread: Pathogens can infect all above-ground parts and overwinter in seed, crop residue, and soil.
Seed transmission efficiency up to 86%.
M. pinodes undergoes both sexual (ascospores via pseudothecia) and asexual (conidia via pycnidia) reproduction, while producing chlamydospores surviving in soil for at least 5 years.
epidemiology: Initial infection results in small purple to black spots that expand with moisture.
Under low temperature and moderate moisture, old pycnidia mature, new pycnidia and perithecia develop, releasing spores.
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses range from 30% to 75% normally, and up to 100% under favorable environmental conditions.
Average field loss in Ethiopia reported at 20-30% or up to 53%.

cultural_management: Crop rotation up to 3 to 4 years to reduce A. pisi and P. medicaginis
Mixed cropping (sowing field pea together with faba bean) reduces infection from 100% to 32%
Use of clean, pathogen-free seeds
Holding severely infected seeds for at least one year before sowing if no seed treatment is used
Residual burial to eliminate soil-borne and residue-borne inoculum

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Successfully lessens the effects of Ascochyta blight when combined with tolerant cultivars.
Successfully lessens the effects of Ascochyta blight when combined with tolerant cultivars.
Successfully lessens the effects of Ascochyta blight when combined with tolerant cultivars.

integrated_management: Combination of tolerant cultivars with chemical treatments

farmer_action_points: Select resistant or moderately resistant varieties
Practice crop rotation and mixed cropping with faba bean
Use clean seeds and avoid planting infected residues near new crops
warnings_and_limitations: Chemical pesticides are often unaffordable for small-scale farmers in impoverished nations.
Foliar fungicide application is challenging after canopy closure as lower leaves and stems become inaccessible.
research_findings: Most field pea genotypes showed susceptible reactions while some showed moderate resistance to Ascochyta blight.
Tolerant lines develop the same high level of disease as susceptible lines but suffer less yield loss due to stronger stems.

documents.causal_agent: Erysiphe pisi (also referred to as Erysiphe polygoni)

general: White powdery dust-like layer on the surface of leaves, petioles, stems, and pods
Yellowed, dwarfed, and deformed leaves
early_symptoms: Small, diffuse spots on leaflets and stipules, usually first appearing on the lowest part of the plant as white powdery spots
advanced_symptoms: Lesions grow and become white to pale gray powdery areas that coalesce and completely cover plant surfaces
Seed discoloration and downgraded seed quality
visual_field_symptoms: White powdery dust-like fungal growth covering leaves, stems, and pods
Yellowing and dwarfing of plant foliage

field_identification: White powdery patches on lower leaves spreading to cover the entire plant surface
diagnostic_methods: Internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequences from rDNA differentiation
Analysis of morphological traits such as mycelioid appendages in E. pisi
differential_diagnosis: Distinguished from E. trifolii and E. baeumleri by having normally mycelioid appendages instead of dichotomously branched ones.

causes_and_risk_factors: Airborne or seed-borne obligate fungus overwinters on infected pea trash
High soil nitrogen availability
Lush pea stands
Late-sown and off-season fields

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Low rainfall (spores are washed away by rain)
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: High soil nitrogen
other_conditions: Warm and dry days with dew formation

disease_development_and_spread: Spores are blown by wind into new crops on warm, dry days with dew formation.
Can completely colonize a plant in 5 to 6 days under favorable conditions.
Conidia from superficial conidiophores or ascospores act as main dispersal propagules.
epidemiology: Rapidly spreads to adjacent areas once a few plants become infected.
More severe in dry heat and late-sown or off-season fields.
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes up to 50–86% loss in field pea growth globally.
Reduces yield by 20–30% at mid-altitude locations.
Average yield losses of 25 to 50% globally and 21–37% in Ethiopia.

cultural_management: Plant early in the growing season or use early-maturing cultivars
Avoid excess fertilizing or use slow-release fertilizers
Locate plants in sunny areas with good ventilation
Overhead sprinkling to wash away spores
biological_management: Use of biological antagonists such as Trichoderma spp., Bacillus subtilis, and Pseudomonas sp.

chemical_management.number_of_applications: Single application (or followed by additional sprays at 14-day intervals)
chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: 68% disease reduction; prevents mildew infection of pods, increases yield, and evens out maturity

integrated_management: Combination of genetic resistance, cultural adjustments, and judicious fungicide applications

farmer_action_points: Plant early-maturing varieties at the start of the season
Monitor fields regularly and apply fungicides at early flowering if infection occurs
Ensure proper plant spacing and sunlight exposure
warnings_and_limitations: Repeated protective fungicide applications can be costly and economically unjustified.
Spores can cause breathing and allergy issues for machinery operators.
research_findings: Genetics of powdery mildew resistance involve major loci: Er1, Er2, and Er3.

documents.search_text: crop Field Pea (Pisum sativum) paper_information title Field Pea (Pisum sativum) Diseases of Major Importance and Their Management in Ethiopia, a Review authors Zenebe Wubshet Hordofa Zelalem Tamiru year 2023 journal_or_source Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries doi_or_identifier 10.11648/j.aff.20231205.11 abstract_summary The paper provides insight into the economic significance, distribution, and current management strategies for major field pea diseases in Ethiopia, highlighting fungal diseases like Ascochyta blight, powdery mildew, downy mildew, Fusarium wilt, and rust. research_objective To provide insight into the economic significance, distribution, and current management strategies for significant field pea diseases as well as to establish future approaches. study_area Ethiopia important_findings Ascochyta blight and powdery mildew are the most severe fungal diseases affecting field pea production in Ethiopia. Ascochyta blight can cause yield losses ranging from 30% to 75% under normal conditions and up to 100% under favorable conditions. Powdery mildew causes yield losses ranging from 50% to 86% globally and 21% to 37% in Ethiopia. Management strategies must focus on cultural practices, host resistance, biological control, and targeted chemical applications integrated into IDM strategies. disease disease_name Powdery Mildew alternative_names disease_type Fungal disease causal_agent Erysiphe pisi (also referred to as Erysiphe polygoni) pathogen_type Fungus affected_plant_parts Leaves Stipules Petioles Stems Pods symptoms general White powdery dust-like layer on the surface of leaves, petioles, stems, and pods Yellowed, dwarfed, and deformed leaves early_symptoms Small, diffuse spots on leaflets and stipules, usually first appearing on the lowest part of the plant as white powdery spots advanced_symptoms Lesions grow and become white to pale gray powdery areas that coalesce and completely cover plant surfaces Seed discoloration and downgraded seed quality visual_field_symptoms White powdery dust-like fungal growth covering leaves, stems, and pods Yellowing and dwarfing of plant foliage identification field_identification White powdery patches on lower leaves spreading to cover the entire plant surface diagnostic_methods Internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequences from rDNA differentiation Analysis of morphological traits such as mycelioid appendages in E. pisi differential_diagnosis Distinguished from E. trifolii and E. baeumleri by having normally mycelioid appendages instead of dichotomously branched ones. causes_and_risk_factors Airborne or seed-borne obligate fungus overwinters on infected pea trash High soil nitrogen availability Lush pea stands Late-sown and off-season fields favorable_conditions temperature 15–25°C humidity Over 70 percent RH rainfall Low rainfall (spores are washed away by rain) soil_conditions High soil nitrogen other_conditions Warm and dry days with dew formation Shade and mild temperatures disease_development_and_spread Spores are blown by wind into new crops on warm, dry days with dew formation. Can completely colonize a plant in 5 to 6 days under favorable conditions. Conidia from superficial conidiophores or ascospores act as main dispersal propagules. epidemiology Rapidly spreads to adjacent areas once a few plants become infected. More severe in dry heat and late-sown or off-season fields. severity_and_yield_loss Causes up to 50–86% loss in field pea growth globally. Reduces yield by 20–30% at mid-altitude locations. Average yield losses of 25 to 50% globally and 21–37% in Ethiopia. management cultural_management Plant early in the growing season or use early-maturing cultivars Avoid excess fertilizing or use slow-release fertilizers Locate plants in sunny areas with good ventilation Overhead sprinkling to wash away spores biological_management Use of biological antagonists such as Trichoderma spp., Bacillus subtilis, and Pseudomonas sp. chemical_management active_ingredient_or_product Tebuconazole dose concentration application_method timing number_of_applications result_reported_in_paper 81% disease reduction active_ingredient_or_product Propiconazole dose concentration application_method timing number_of_applications result_reported_in_paper 78% disease reduction active_ingredient_or_product Triadimefon dose concentration application_method timing Single application at early flowering number_of_applications Single application (or followed by additional sprays at 14-day intervals) result_reported_in_paper 68% disease reduction; prevents mildew infection of pods, increases yield, and evens out maturity integrated_management Combination of genetic resistance, cultural adjustments, and judicious fungicide applications resistant_or_tolerant_varieties GPHA-12 GPHA-9 GPHA-22 GPHA-44 GPHA-19 GPHA-68 GPHA-58 GPHA-28 GPHA-59 GPHA-46 GPHA-24 susceptible_varieties prevention Early planting Using early-maturing cultivars Avoiding excessive nitrogen fertilization farmer_action_points Plant early-maturing varieties at the start of the season Monitor fields regularly and apply fungicides at early flowering if infection occurs Ensure proper plant spacing and sunlight exposure warnings_and_limitations Repeated protective fungicide applications can be costly and economically unjustified. Spores can cause breathing and allergy issues for machinery operators. research_findings Genetics of powdery mildew resistance involve major loci: Er1, Er2, and Er3. Gene Er1 is frequently employed in breeding programs for resistance. source_pages 5 6 7 8

general: Water soaked lesions move from tip to downwards on the edges of leaves
Gradually, symptoms turn into yellow and straw coloured stripes with wavy margins
In Kresek (wilt) phase, leaves roll completely, droop and plants die completely
early_symptoms: Symptoms start appearing from the tip and progress downwards in the form of inverted 'V' shape
advanced_symptoms: Affected grains have discoloured spots surrounded by water soaked areas
visual_field_symptoms: BLB infected rice field shows yellow and straw coloured stripes on the sides of the leaves starting from tip

field_identification: Inverted V shape symptom on leaves
Ooze test: a yellowish, opaque, turbid drop of bacterial ooze comes out from cut edge of infected leaf when immersed in water
diagnostic_methods: Ooze test in water
differential_diagnosis: Late season potassium deficiency resembles BLB, but BLB yields bacterial ooze in water test

causes_and_risk_factors: Excess N application

cultural_management: Balanced fertilizer application with split application of N
Potash application
Alternate drying and flooding in the field help in reducing infection
biological_management: Spray fresh cow dung extracts (1 kg cow dung in 5 liter water)

chemical_management.application_method: seed soaking in 2 liters of water

chemical_management.dose: plantomycin @ 1 g L-1 of water or (streptocycline (0.15g) + copper oxy chloride (1 g) per liter of water)

prevention: Treat seed by soaking in water containing streptocycline and captan
Hot water seed treatment at 53 deg C for 30 min after 12 hrs soak
farmer_action_points: Perform ooze test by cutting leaf and immersing in water

general: Spots appear in the leaves and glumes, seedlings, sheaths, stems and grains
Infected seedlings have small, circular or oval, brown lesions
Fully developed lesion on older leaves is oval, brown with gray or whitish center with reddish brown margin
Black or dark lesions with a velvety aspect develop on glumes
Black discoloration or brown lesions appear on grains
Black discoloration of roots
advanced_symptoms: Under severe infection, lesions may coalesce, killing large areas of affected leaves
Seedlings become stunted or die under severe infestation
visual_field_symptoms: Severely infected plant showing oval, brown spot with gray/whitish center with reddish brown margin

field_identification: Small, circular, dark brown lesions on leaves
differential_diagnosis: Potassium deficient plants show brown spots in older leaves, but spots are dusky without any distinct margin

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Soil deficit in Mn

cultural_management: Use healthy seeds from disease free crops
Adopt deep summer ploughing
Apply balanced NPK with zinc and manganese
Apply additional K (20% extra) at appearance of disease

chemical_management.dose: propiconazole @ 1 mL L-1 or 0.4% mancozeb or 0.25% ziram or 0.2% carbendazim

prevention: Treat seeds with captan or thiram

general: Disease occurs at all crop stages (nursery, tillering, flowering)
Elliptical or spindle shaped lesions with brown border and grayish/ashy center on leaves
Collar region marked by rusty brown appearance at junction of leaf blade and leaf sheath
Stems turn dark brown to blackish color at node (Node blast)
Black necrotic lesions around the base of panicles resulting in breakdown of panicles and formation of chaffy grains (Neck blast)
advanced_symptoms: Under favorable conditions, lesions enlarge and coalesce and entire leaf withers
Entire leaf blade dries up in collar blast
Stem becomes weak and breaks easily in node blast
visual_field_symptoms: Spindle shaped lesions on leaves with brown border and grayish centre

field_identification: Spindle-shaped leaf lesions with gray centers
Node blackening and breakage
Neck blast panicle breakage

causes_and_risk_factors: Soils rich in N / fields applied with excess N

cultural_management: Use healthy seeds collected from disease free crops
Apply balanced dose of nitrogenous fertilizer in 3-4 splits (80 kg N ha-1)
Weed out alternate hosts (Cynodron sp. and Paspalum sp.)
Maintain standing water in the field
biological_management: Bael leaf extract (25 g fresh leaves L-1 water)
Tulsi leaf extract (25 g fresh young leaves L-1 water)
Neem leaf extract (200 g fresh leaves L-1 water)

general: Small, dark-green and water-soaked streaks between veins from tillering to booting stage
Streaks enlarge to become yellowish gray and translucent then turn light brown or yellowish brown
Large areas of leaf may become dry due to numerous streaks
early_symptoms: Small dark-green water-soaked streaks between veins
visual_field_symptoms: Patch of yellowish gray interveinal streaks on early infected leaf

field_identification: Interveinal streaks turning yellowish gray
Bacterial exudates from infected cut leaves when placed in water
diagnostic_methods: Ooze test in water
differential_diagnosis: Potassium deficiency starts from leaf tip and margin and progresses toward midrib, whereas BLS is interveinal streaks
At later stage indistinguishable from BLB, but BLB has inverted V shape appearance

cultural_management: Apply balanced dose of NPK
Additional potash application in the field helps in reducing infection
Avoid field to field irrigation
Avoid clipping of seedlings at transplanting
biological_management: Spray fresh cow dung extract (1 kg cow dung in 5 liters water) thrice at eight days interval

chemical_management.application_method: seed soaking in 2 liters of water

chemical_management.timing: upon onset of symptoms, twice at 8 days interval

prevention: Hot water treatment of seeds for 12 hours at 53 deg C for 30 minutes

general: Appears in later growth stages in late tillering or early internode elongation stage
Initial symptoms on sheaths of lower leaves or just below leaf collar near water line as small, ellipsoidal or ovoid, greenish-gray and water-soaked lesions
Later lesions occur with grayish white center and light brown to dark brown margin
White sclerotia of mustard seed size found on infected sheaths
early_symptoms: Small, ellipsoidal or ovoid, greenish-gray and water-soaked lesions on lower leaf sheaths
advanced_symptoms: Lesions dry and become grayish-white to tan with brownish borders and may coalesce forming bigger lesions, causing death of whole leaf
Severely infected plants produce poorly filled or empty grains, especially on lower portion of panicles
visual_field_symptoms: Rice plant showing sheath blight lesions on leaf sheath
Rice plant showing sheath blight lesions with brownish border and grayish white centre

field_identification: Ellipsoidal lesions on sheaths with grayish-white centers and dark brown margins
Presence of mustard-seed-sized white sclerotia

other_conditions: early heading and grain filling stages favor rapid development

cultural_management: Adopt deep summer ploughing so sclerotia in soil are exposed to hot sunlight
Incorporate green manure (Sesbania sp.) in sheath blight endemic areas
Do not transplant more than 3 seedlings hill-1
Maintain field sanitation by removing weeds

Grey blotches on seeds

general: Light to reddish purple angular to irregular lesions on both leaf surfaces at beginning of seed set
Upper leaves sometimes have light purple appearance making them leathery and dark
Rapid chlorosis and necrosis of leaf tissues resulting in defoliation from upper young leaves
Veinal necrosis and blightening of younger upper leaves over large area
Reddish purple to reddish black slightly sunken lesions on stem, petiole and pod
Heavily infected stems have dull gray to dark brown appearance and dry up 7-10 days prematurely
Seeds develop pink to dark purple coloration
Low seed germination, shriveled and discolored cotyledons, seedling death
early_symptoms: Light to reddish purple angular to irregular lesions on leaves at seed set
advanced_symptoms: Rapid chlorosis/necrosis, veinal necrosis, upper leaf blightening
Premature stem drying
Purple stained seeds
visual_field_symptoms: Leathery dark upper leaves with light purple appearance
Blightening of younger upper leaves
Pink to dark purple stained seeds

field_identification: Purple angular lesions on leaves
Blightening of upper young leaves
Characteristic purple stain on seeds

causes_and_risk_factors: High humidity especially at flowering stage on early maturing cultivars
Pathogen survival in seeds and surface crop debris

other_conditions: Flowering stage in early maturing cultivars

disease_development_and_spread: Pathogen overwinters in diseased leaves, stems, and seeds
Infects plants at flowering stage
Secondary infection from conidia produced on infected plants
Fungus reaches seed coat from pods producing purple stain
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes 15-30% yield loss
Reduced seed germination and market value due to staining

cultural_management: Use of clean & certified seeds
Cultivation of resistant varieties like JS 80-21 & Bragg

farmer_action_points: Use certified clean seeds
Seed treatment with recommended fungicides

general: White cottony mycelium with reddish brown to dark brown mustard size sclerotia on the surface
Attacks collar region or just below soil surface
Damping off in younger and collar rot in older plants resulting in drooping or wilting
early_symptoms: Damping off in younger plants
White cottony growth at stem base
advanced_symptoms: Wilting and drooping of plants
Development of mustard-sized brown sclerotia on surface
visual_field_symptoms: Cottony white mycelium and brown sclerotia at the base of the stem
Drooping and wilting of plants

field_identification: White cottony mycelium with mustard-sized brown sclerotia at stem base
Wilting and damping off

causes_and_risk_factors: Hot and humid conditions
Soil-borne sclerotia persisting through soil, crop residue and weeds
disease_development_and_spread: Sclerotia perpetuate through soil, crop residue, and weeds
Sclerotia can flow with water to other parts of the field to infect the crop

cultural_management: Field sanitation, rouging and burning of infected plants check spread of disease
Crop rotation with maize or sorghum
Deep summer ploughing to a depth of 15-20 cm to reduce pathogen
Use tolerant variety NRC 37
biological_management: Trichoderma @ 5 g/kg seed

farmer_action_points: Treat seeds with Vitavax or Trichoderma
Perform deep summer ploughing
Uproot and bury infected plants showing cottony growth at stem base

Leaves droop down, dry, and remain attached to plants

Abundant minute black sclerotia beneath outer skin with silvery grey colour

Premature death of infected seedlings
advanced_symptoms: Silvery grey stem with abundant minute black sclerotia beneath outer skin

Dried leaves hanging/attached to plants

field_identification: Silvery grey stem with minute black sclerotia beneath the outer skin

causes_and_risk_factors: Dry conditions, low soil moisture
Temperature ranging from 25 to 35 C

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Low soil moisture

disease_development_and_spread: Soil and seed borne disease

cultural_management: Irrigation during low soil moisture (drought condition) especially at flowering to pod-fill stage
Crop rotation with cereals or mixed cropping
Balanced use of fertilizer and proper seed rate
Use tolerant varieties like NRC 2, NRC 37, JS 71-05, AMS 5-18, JS 20-98, MACS 13
Sowing at raised bed or broad bed with basal application of Zinc Sulphate @ 25 kg/ha along with Boron @ 0.5 kg/ha

Apply basal zinc sulphate and boron on raised/broad beds

Leaves become ragged when dead areas are torn away by wind
Severe infection results in defoliation
Small reddish brown slightly raised spots on pods in highly susceptible cultivars

advanced_symptoms: Lesions merge into irregular mottled brown areas
Ragged leaves and defoliation
visual_field_symptoms: Spots with dark centers and pale green haloes
Ragged torn leaves

field_identification: Pale green spots with raised centers and haloes on leaves
Ragged leaves due to wind tearing dead tissue

Spreads through water splashing or wind-blown rain
Warm weather conditions and frequent rains during cropping season

Enters through natural openings and wounds
Spreads via water splashing and wind-blown rain

Follow crop rotations with cereals and maize
Use balanced dose of fertilizer specially potash 40-80 Kg/ha

Follow crop rotation with cereals and maize

general: Small yellow spots or patches on the green lamina of young leaves that develop into golden yellow mosaic or bright yellow mosaic symptoms.
Complete yellowing of the leaves as infection progresses.
Significantly delays plant maturity, decreases flower production, and hampers pod formation.
Severely affected plants produce undersized and immature seeds.
early_symptoms: Small yellow spots or patches on the green lamina of young leaves.
advanced_symptoms: Complete yellowing of leaves, necrotic centre within yellow spots in some varieties, small and distorted pods, and plant death before seed set in severe cases.
visual_field_symptoms: Golden yellow mosaic or bright yellow mosaic patterns on leaves.

field_identification: Observation of small yellow spots/patches on young leaves developing into bright yellow mosaic symptoms.

causes_and_risk_factors: Presence of viruliferous whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci)
Weed hosts acting as reservoirs such as Croton sparsiflorus, Acalypha indica, Eclipta alba
disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) and through grafting; not transmitted through seed, soil, or sap.
epidemiology: The epidemic is increasing every year in all urdbean and mungbean cultivating areas because of its vector whitefly.
severity_and_yield_loss: Average yield loss varies from 10 to 100%, depending on the stage of infection and genotype.

cultural_management: Crop rotation with non-host plants and maintaining field hygiene by removing infected plant debris.
Adjusting sowing dates and plant population.
Intercropping with sorghum or maize.
Rogueing infected plants up to 45 days.
integrated_management: Resistant varieties
Vector control using insecticidal sprays, reflective mulches, and yellow sticky traps @ 12 traps per hectare
Crop rotation and sanitation
Seed treatment
Sowing manipulation and plant density
Rogueing
Foliar sprays

prevention: Use of disease-free seeds and resistant varieties
farmer_action_points: Install Yellow Sticky Traps @ 12 traps per hectare.
Remove infected plants up to 45 days after sowing.

general: White powdery patches appear on leaves and other green areas, later becoming dull in colour and covering lower leaf surfaces.

Heavily infected plant parts become distorted and shrivelled, leading to yellowing of foliage and premature defoliation.
early_symptoms: White powdery patches appear on leaves and other green areas.
advanced_symptoms: Complete coverage of leaf surfaces by whitish powdery growth, distorted and shrivelled parts, premature defoliation, and forced premature maturity.

field_identification: Presence of white powdery patches on leaves and green parts.

causes_and_risk_factors: Older plants are more susceptible than young plants.
disease_development_and_spread: Survives as cleistothecia in infected plant debris or as oidial form on alternative hosts like Lathyrus sativa, Vicia faba, Vigna ungulate. Spread by air-borne conidia and rain splash.
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss varies from 9% to 50% in farmers' fields.

Timely planting
Weed management

general: Abnormal enlargement of leaves, curling, crinkling, or rugosity.
Initial symptoms appear on the third trifoliate as light green colour with slight expansion of leaflets and raised inter-venal areas.
Subsequent leaves display malformations, increased size, and crinkled lamina surface up to 1.5 times healthy leaves.
Shortened internodes resulting in clumping of apical growth and bushy inflorescences.
Delayed flowering, malformed small flower buds that fail to open, reduced pollen fertility and pod setting.
early_symptoms: Initial noticeable symptom appears in the third trifoliate, exhibiting a light green colour with slight expansion of leaflets and raised inter-venal areas.
advanced_symptoms: Leaf malformations, crinkled lamina, shortened internodes, bushy inflorescences, and reduced pod setting.
visual_field_symptoms: Crinkled, enlarged leaves with curled margins and clumped apical growth.

other_conditions: Kharif season crops are highly susceptible

severity_and_yield_loss: Up to 100% yield losses depending upon variety and season; complete seed production failure in early-infected plants.

cultural_management: Use of disease-free seeds
Removing all collateral weed hosts from the field and rouging out infected plants
Cultivating resistant urdbean varieties

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Can reduce whitefly populations and the incidence of leaf crinkle.
Reported to reduce the severity of ULCV infection.

integrated_management: Use of disease-free seeds, weed removal and rogueing, hot water treatment, resistant varieties, foliar sprays of insecticides/botanicals, and nutrient application (nitrogen, potash, phosphorus, boron, zinc, and NAA).

prevention: Hot water seed treatment at 52°C for 20–30 minutes
farmer_action_points: Remove collateral weed hosts and rogue out infected plants.
research_findings: Application of nitrogen, potash, phosphorus, boron, zinc, and naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) showed effectiveness in reducing ULCV infection.

Watermelon cultivation is affected by several major fungal, bacterial, and viral diseases. Chemical methods must be used judiciously to avoid pathogen resistance and environmental pollution. disease disease_name Watermelon mosaic alternative_names disease_type Viral disease causal_agent general: Appears as a mass of yellow to orange urediniospores erupting from pustules arranged in long, narrow stripes on leaves, leaf sheaths, glumes and awns.
early_symptoms: Disease starts with small patches or foci of infection.
advanced_symptoms: Spreads rapidly under congenial weather in long narrow stripes between veins.
visual_field_symptoms: Orange dust comes out on fingers and clothing when touching infected leaves.
Starts in small patches or foci.

field_identification: Look for yellow to orange pustules arranged in long, narrow stripes between leaf veins.
Spores rub off as orange dust on fingers and clothing.

causes_and_risk_factors: High dose of Nitrogen fertilizers
Growing single susceptible variety over large areas
disease_development_and_spread: Spreads rapidly from initial infection foci under congenial weather.

cultural_management: Grow recently released resistant varieties recommended for the zone.
Grow yellow rust tolerant varieties and avoid use of one particular variety over large areas.
Use balanced and recommended quantity of fertilisers and avoid high dose of Nitrogen.

chemical_management.timing: Immediately on appearance of disease to avoid further spread from initial infection foci

prevention: Keep strict watch on appearance of the disease.
farmer_action_points: Inspect fields for small patches of yellow stripes on leaves.
Spray propiconazole @ 0.1% immediately upon detection.
warnings_and_limitations: Most recommended varieties for NWPZ and NHZ do not carry high level of resistance, hence chemical sprays are needed.

general: Small, circular to oval pustules with orange to light brown dusty spores on upper surface of leaves and on leaf sheaths in heavy infections.
visual_field_symptoms: Pustules mainly confined to the upper surface and irregularly distributed on leaves.

field_identification: Small, circular to oval orange to light brown dusty pustules on upper leaf surfaces.

causes_and_risk_factors: High dose of nitrogen fertilizers
Planting a single variety over large areas

cultural_management: Grow recommended varieties for the zone.
Grow leaf rust tolerant varieties and avoid single variety over large areas.
Use balanced and recommended quantity of fertilisers and avoid high dose of nitrogen.

general: Large orange-brown pustules oval or elongated in shape on stems and sometimes both sides of leaves and leaf sheaths.
advanced_symptoms: Presence of silver-colored ruptured epidermis above pustules.
Rupture of pustules releases a powdery mass of brick red colored urediniospores.
visual_field_symptoms: Oval or elongated orange-brown pustules on stems with silver ruptured epidermis.

field_identification: Large, oval or elongated orange-brown pustules on stems with ruptured silvery epidermis releasing brick-red powdery spores.

causes_and_risk_factors: High dose of nitrogen
Growing single variety over large areas

cultural_management: Grow recommended varieties for the zone.
Grow stem rust tolerant varieties and avoid single variety over large areas.
Use balanced and recommended quantity of fertilisers and avoid high dose of nitrogen.

chemical_management.timing: Immediate spraying of affected areas upon appearance

prevention: Keep strict watch on appearance of the disease.
farmer_action_points: Check stems for elongated pustules and apply propiconazole @ 0.1% immediately.

general: Extremely difficult to diagnose in the field because few kernels in an ear head get infected.
Grains are either partially affected or in severe cases whole grain is converted into black powder of bunt spores.
visual_field_symptoms: Normally noticed after threshing where grains show black powdery mass.

field_identification: Difficult to identify in field; detected after threshing by partial or complete conversion of kernels into black powder.

causes_and_risk_factors: Frequent rains during ear head emergence.

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Frequent rains during ear head emergence

cultural_management: Use certified or disease-free seed.
Follow crop rotation and avoid growing wheat for 2-3 years in highly infected fields.
Zero tillage helps in reducing Karnal bunt incidence.

chemical_management.timing: At the time of 50% flowering; repeat after 15 days if it rains

prevention: Use certified or disease free seed.
farmer_action_points: Inspect threshed grain for black powdery kernels.
Spray propiconazole @ 0.1% at 50% flowering in prone areas.

general: Small, dark brown lesions 1 to 2 mm long without chlorotic margin.
Lesions extend very quickly into oval to elongated blotches, light brown to dark brown, coalescing and causing death of the leaf.
early_symptoms: Small, dark brown lesions 1 to 2 mm long without chlorotic margin.
advanced_symptoms: Oval to elongated blotches that coalesce leading to leaf death.
Shrivelled grain and black point (dark staining of embryo end of seed) if spikelets are affected.
visual_field_symptoms: Dark brown small lesions extending into larger blotches causing leaf death.

field_identification: Look for small dark brown lesions without chlorotic margins expanding into blighted blotches on leaves.

causes_and_risk_factors: Humid and warmer areas

cultural_management: Cultivation of recommended resistant varieties.

prevention: Use seed treatment with carboxin or carboxin+thiram.
farmer_action_points: Treat seeds before planting.
Spray difenoconazole or triadimefon upon initial symptom appearance.

general: Superficial greyish small patches of white cottony growth on leaves, sheath, stem, and even on ear head.
early_symptoms: Superficial greyish small patches of white cottony growth.
advanced_symptoms: White cottony growth covers the whole leaf and other aerial parts.
White patches turn brownish to dull tan color late in the season due to formation of cleistothecia.
visual_field_symptoms: White cottony fungal patches on leaves and stems turning brownish later.

field_identification: White cottony or greyish patches on leaves, sheaths, and stems.

causes_and_risk_factors: Excessively dense stands
Cooler areas and hilly regions

cultural_management: Use recommended quantity of seed to avoid excessively dense stands.

chemical_management.timing: At appearance of disease in disease prone areas

prevention: Avoid excessively dense stands by using recommended seed rates.
farmer_action_points: Look for white cottony patches on foliage and apply triadimefon 25% WP @ 0.1%.

general: Spore mass covered with a delicate silvery membrane of host origin which usually ruptures before complete emergence of ears, exposing dark olive-brown powdery mass of spores.
early_symptoms: Smutted spike emerges from boot leaf a few days earlier than healthy plants.
advanced_symptoms: Normal spikelets replaced entirely by dark olive-brown powdery mass of spores.
visual_field_symptoms: Black/dark brown powdery heads emerging earlier than healthy ears.

field_identification: Ears replaced by dark olive-brown powdery spore masses emerging earlier than healthy plants.

causes_and_risk_factors: Cooler wheat growing areas

cultural_management: Use disease free seed.
Rouge out and destroy infected tillers.

farmer_action_points: Rouge out infected tillers in the field.
Treat seeds with carboxin, carbendazim, or tebuconazole before planting.

general: Black narrow elongated blisters appear on leaves between veins; ruptured blisters expose black spore balls and split leaves into ribbons.
Black streaks on stunted stems with dwarfed internodes.
advanced_symptoms: Infected plants stunted and spindly with more tillers (grass-like appearance).
Inflorescence stunted, distorted, frequently sterile, bearing black streaks.
Spike development stops before head emerges from leaf whorl (no seeds produced).
visual_field_symptoms: Black narrow blisters on leaves splitting into ribbons, stunted plants with grass-like appearance.

field_identification: Black narrow blisters on leaves splitting into ribbons and black streaks on stems of stunted, tillering plants.

causes_and_risk_factors: Sandy soils

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy soils

cultural_management: Use disease free seed.

prevention: Use disease free seed and treat seed before planting.
farmer_action_points: Inspect sandy soil fields for stunted plants with black leaf streaks.
Apply seed treatments using carboxin or tebuconazole.

Spike development stops before head emerges from leaf whorl (no seeds produced). visual_field_symptoms Black narrow blisters on leaves splitting into ribbons, stunted plants with grass-like appearance. identification field_identification Black narrow blisters on leaves splitting into ribbons and black streaks on stems of stunted, tillering plants. diagnostic_methods differential_diagnosis causes_and_risk_factors Sandy soils favorable_conditions temperature humidity rainfall soil_conditions Sandy soils other_conditions disease_development_and_spread epidemiology severity_and_yield_loss management cultural_management Use disease free seed. biological_management chemical_management active_ingredient_or_product carboxin 75 WP dose 2.5 g/kg seed concentration application_method seed treatment timing Before sowing number_of_applications 1 result_reported_in_paper active_ingredient_or_product tebuconazole 2DS dose 1.25 g/kg concentration application_method seed treatment timing Before sowing number_of_applications 1 result_reported_in_paper integrated_management resistant_or_tolerant_varieties susceptible_varieties prevention Use disease free seed and treat seed before planting. farmer_action_points Inspect sandy soil fields for stunted plants with black leaf streaks. general: Infects leaves, spikes, and grains.
early_symptoms: Water soaked spots with deep green color on leaves turning into brown boat-shaped necrotic spots.
advanced_symptoms: Glumes show elliptical lesions with reddish brown to dark grey margins and white to light brown center.
Ears rendered shrunken, shrivelled and deformed with no grain filling.
visual_field_symptoms: Boat-shaped brown necrotic spots on leaves and bleached/deformed spikes.

field_identification: Brown boat-shaped spots on leaves and bleached, shrunken spikes.

causes_and_risk_factors: Warmer and humid climate
Grassy weeds acting as secondary hosts (Eleusine indica, Leersia, Echinochloa, Brachiaria, Digitaria, Lolium, Cenchrus, Chloris)
disease_development_and_spread: Grassy weeds act as secondary hosts and spread the disease in wheat.
severity_and_yield_loss: Heavy yield loss or total crop failure

cultural_management: Use certified and disease free seed.
Use resistant wheat varieties.
Regularly remove and destroy weeds and grasses in and around the wheat field.

farmer_action_points: Clear grassy weeds from field borders.
Spray trifloxystrobin + tebuconazole upon infection.
warnings_and_limitations: Till date the disease is not reported from India (noted as present in Bangladesh and South America).

documents.document_id: wheat__fusarium head blight or head scab
documents.disease_name: Fusarium head blight or head scab

general: Small, water soaked spots at base or middle of glumes, rachis or first floret spreading within the earhead.
early_symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on glumes, rachis, or florets.
advanced_symptoms: Premature whitening or bleaching of ear head.
White, pinky-salmon mass of spores on infected glumes and spikelets under warm and moist conditions.
Developing grain turns shrunken, shrivelled, rough surfaced, discoloured soft-gray, chalky white to light-brown ('tombstones').
visual_field_symptoms: Premature bleaching of ear heads and pinkish-salmon spore masses.

field_identification: Bleached ear heads with possible pinkish spore masses and shrunken chalky kernels ('tombstones').

causes_and_risk_factors: Humid and subhumid climate

cultural_management: Use certified and disease free seed.
Use resistant wheat varieties.

prevention: Use certified and disease-free seeds and resistant varieties.
farmer_action_points: Inspect fields for bleached heads and treat seeds before planting.

documents.document_id: wheat__hill bunt or stinking smut or common bunt
documents.disease_name: Hill Bunt or Stinking Smut or Common bunt

general: Bunted heads are slender, bluish-green and stay greener longer than healthy heads.
Bunt balls change to dull gray-brown at maturity.
Grains full of black powder giving a foul smell resembling rotten fish.
advanced_symptoms: Fragile covering of bunt balls ruptures at harvest, producing clouds of spores.
visual_field_symptoms: Foul smell resembling rotten fish in the field, bluish-green slender heads.

field_identification: Identified by a distinct foul smell of rotten fish in the field and bluish-green slender heads with gray-brown bunt balls.

disease_development_and_spread: Spores released in clouds when bunt balls rupture at harvest.

cultural_management: Use certified and disease free seed.
Sowing of disease resistant varieties.

prevention: Use certified seed and seed treatments.
farmer_action_points: Check for rotten-fish odor in fields and treat seeds with carboxin or carbendazim.
